Lessons learned
Four lessons came out of writing this design, and they generalise beyond this plant to any condition-
monitoring build inside a regulated OT perimeter. They are listed below as their own headed points.
One-way egress before clever analytics
The DCS read path was our first design risk, because a direct control-network connection degrades plant
operations. We settled on hardware one-way egress into a DMZ OPC UA collector, with a signed zone-and-
conduit diagram as a phase one deliverable. A condition monitoring system that can touch the trip philosophy
is worth less than one that cannot.
Licence and fit before model size
We chose MOMENT-1, an MIT-licensed time-series foundation model, for anomaly detection because it runs
zero-shot on a 48 GB-class site card, and IBM Granite 4.2 8B under Apache-2.0 for report drafting. The larger
forecaster alternatives were rejected on licence cleanliness and memory envelope, not accuracy claims.
Check what fits the card and the contract before comparing leaderboards.
Tune thresholds only on provable history
Recovered pre-fire condition history may be too sparse to baseline on, which quietly undermines every
threshold downstream. The design requires a migration report stating recovered-versus-fresh per channel,
and phase two thresholds tune only on channels with provable history. Write the sparsity down before you
calibrate against it.
Alert budget, heartbeat and the watched watcher
Alert flooding trains operators to ignore the platform, so the design carries a gate of 2 false alerts per week
and separates channel health from process alarms. The 2003 blackout history pushed us further: positive
heartbeat and freshness indicators on the operator surface, so the platform's own failure is visible. A system
that only reports exceptions fails silently.
Wire compliance in phase one, not later
NEPRA's IT/OT Security Regulations 2022 demand five years of tamper-evident logs and quarterly PowerCERT
reporting, and retrofitting that trail is a breach waiting to happen. We wired the logs and the reporting
schedule from phase one alongside the functional scope. Regulatory duties are architecture inputs, not
paperwork after go-live.

What is still open

Four questions could not be closed from the requirement, and the design states each one rather than
papering over it. The first is fusion: no reference architecture was assigned to this domain, so the domain brief
is the only fusion input and the design proceeds on it alone. Settling it would either confirm the asset-to-alert-
to-work-order pattern or pull in a published architecture with its own defaults. The second is the sovereignty
posture, which the requirement does not state, so nothing in this design assumes one; fixing it would settle
where the mirror-archive master lives and who signs the model updates. The third is the plant CMMS or EAM,
which is domain-typical and not named in the requirement, so it is to be confirmed with the operator and
carries no price weight until it is. The fourth is the agentic work surface, which is offered and not committed,
pending the engineer's confirmation; confirming it would add a fifth surface and change the review loop's
shape. The table below carries the open questions and what settling each one would change.

Conclusion
The design is a condition-monitoring and diagnostics platform for the rehabilitated STG-1 and the new 280
MW generator at the operator's combined cycle plant, built as eight sources feeding four adapters into one
ontology of ten objects, grounded by eight services and opened through four surfaces. It reads the upgraded
DCS, the restored 3500 rack and the generator's winding and hydrogen detection through a one-way OPC UA
path, turns anomalies into severity-ranked alerts with prescribed actions, and runs entirely on the operator's
own hardware under the NEPRA Security of IT and OT Regulations 2022. Two pretrained open-weight models,
MOMENT-1 and IBM Granite 4.2 8B, do the detection and the drafting, sized to a single 48 GB site card with
no training run and no cloud.
Running it somewhere else would take three things. A domain brief for the new asset class, since the design
inherits its asset-to-alert-to-work-order pattern and latency discipline from the brief rather than from a
reference architecture. A regulatory pass, since the NEPRA duties that shaped the logging, the one-way path
and the reporting cadence are jurisdiction-specific. And an import-cycle answer, since the mirror-archive unit
of change control and the spares sizing exist because this plant sits roughly 600 km from the port. The shape
of the system, one-way reads, a typed object model, alerts with owners, survives the move; the numbers in it
do not, and would need to be derived again.

title: Consist Watch: Executing the Operator's Own Fault Logic Across a 225-Car Commuter Fleet
text:
Consist Watch: Executing the Operator's Own
RAIL & TRANSPORTATION · SYSTEM DESIGN

Fault Logic Across a 225-Car Commuter Fleet
Consist Watch is the rail fleet condition monitoring system we designed for a rail and
transportation operator in the United States: 64 named signals per car, the operator's
own fault-logic table, severity-routed locomotive fault detection alerts, and an agentic
work surface over a fleet ontology. This post explains the hardware envelope, the
telemetry path, the data layer and the model choices mechanism by mechanism.
CodeNinja Engineering Team, Forward Deployed Engineering 2026-10-14 20 min read 4,555 words
14 figures

Introduction

A fault on a commuter train becomes visible to the organisation in one of three ways: a crew calls it in over the
radio, a yard employee notices it during a walk-round, or the car fails in service and the mechanical desk
learns about it from the disruption. Across a 225-car fleet, none of those paths involves reading the car.
Across rail transport, defects that go undetected can quietly grow until they cause catastrophic failure, as a
University of Birmingham doctoral study of integrated railway remote condition monitoring puts it, which is
why engineers keep searching for ways to catch developing faults early.
We designed a rail fleet condition monitoring system for a rail and transportation operator in the United States
that closes that gap. The constraints were fixed before we started. The modules ride the car system routers
already installed on each car for cellular service, so the telemetry design inherits their network address
translation and port behaviour rather than adding new connectivity. Compute is contractor-hosted in the
United States, with no server room on the property and no perimeter to defend, which makes role-based
accounts with multi-factor authentication the primary control surface. The hardware half is bounded by the
operator's own envelope: 8 by 8 by 8 inches, IP62, 30-year corrosion protection, 24 to 48 VDC from the
vehicle battery, electronics built to the EN 50155 railway electronics standard, and materials certified to CFR
238 because this is FRA-regulated commuter stock. The design holds 13 months of history over 64 signals
per car and proceeds through a 3-car prototype before the 222-car rollout.
This blog describes the design in the order it was built. It covers how the operation runs today, why the
systems already in place cannot answer the question the mechanical desk actually asks, the layered
architecture from surfaces to storage, the fleet ontology and its 14 objects, how telemetry moves from a
moving car to the cloud, the inference path from a raw reading to a fault closed in the ledger, the two models
and the electronics class behind them, how the design was reasoned, and how delivery and coverage are
evaluated.

Background: how this operation runs
The operation is a commuter rail fleet of 225 cars running in the United States under Federal Railroad
Administration regulation, which means the stock is commuter equipment governed by CFR 238 for fire
certification of materials. Each car already carries its own car system, a set of electronics with cellular routers
installed for existing services, and that car system exposes 64 named signals: 32 digital at 0 to 48 VDC and
32 analog channels. Today nothing reads those signals continuously. A 3-axis accelerometer supplied by the
contractor and GPS data over the car system's ethernet connection complete what the design has to work
with on the vehicle side.
The people are a mechanical desk controller at the control center, yard employees at the outlying yards, and
staff at a center and an office. The plan stages ten places in total, of which the control center, the yard, three
in-service sites, a route segment, the center and the office sit under the system boundary shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1 shows the customer's world and the platform's edge: one named external system, the car system,
feeds the design, and the mechanical desk controller and yard employee roles work what it produces.

The physical conditions are a winter-to-summer spread of -10 to 170 degrees F, body-mounted shock and
vibration on rail stock, and cellular coverage that comes and goes as the cars move. Nothing is wired to train
control or positive train control; the design builds no interface there. Figure 2 shows the operation at steady
state on its own terrain, every staged asset watched continuously, with active faults across the fleet running
at its nominal of zero faults. That steady state is what the system is designed to hold, and to leave quickly
when a reading crosses its threshold.

Figure 1:    The customer's world and the platform's boundary: 1 named systems feed it, 1 roles work it, 7 of
the 10 places the plan staged sit under it.

Figure 2:  The simulation at steady state, drawn on the site's own terrain: every asset the plan staged,
watched continuously, with active faults across the fleet running at its nominal.

The problem
The 64 signals on each car exist and are named, but they are read only when a car happens to be in the shop
with a diagnostic connected. The car system itself carries cellular connectivity, yet it was built for its own
services, not for streaming telemetry, so it has never carried channel data off the vehicle. The mechanical
desk therefore sees service disruptions and crew reports. Yard employees see what a walk-round reveals. The
accelerometer and GPS signals that would show locked axles, wheel slip or hard couplings are simply not
recorded anywhere.
No existing system answers the question the desk actually asks: which cars have active faults right now,
across the whole 225-car fleet, ranked so the desk knows who acts on what. There is no real time fleet health
dashboard, no severity-routed alerting by email and text, no history that would show a thermocouple drifting
across a season, and no record of where slippery rail concentrates on the route. Thirteen months of history
over 64 channels on 225 cars does not exist in any system the operator runs today.
The cost is faults that arrive late, arrive without context, or do not arrive at all. Alerts that do reach the desk
are undifferentiated by severity, and the industry has seen where that ends: a federal investigation into the
East Palestine derailment documented alerts reaching a desk with no capacity to act on them. The technical
problem, stated plainly, is instrumenting 225 cars continuously through routers never designed for it,
buffering through coverage gaps on moving stock, and turning 64 raw signals per car into a small number of
alerts a desk and its yards will actually treat seriously.

Design goals
The requirement set four goals for this rail fleet condition monitoring system, and each one is hard for a
reason specific to this fleet.
The first goal is completeness against the operator's own fault definitions. Each car already names 64 signals,
32 digital and 32 analog, and the requirement carries its own fault-logic table, so the design executes that
table rather than inventing a detection model around it. The hard part is that the analogs arrive raw and need
conditioning. A mis-scaled thermocouple or accelerometer would silently poison every trend built on it, so the
plan calibrates every conditioned channel against known references during prototype commissioning and
records per-channel provenance.
The second goal is visibility where people act. Active faults must be legible at the control centre mechanical
desk and at the outlying yards, as subsecond fleet-wide views across 225 cars, with email and text alerts
routed by severity and tracked to acknowledgement. The hazard here is alert fatigue, and the plan took the
alert-obligation rule from the East Palestine case study: every tier names who acts, when, and with what
authority, and the alert budget is agreed with the desk during the 6-month tuning phase.
The third goal is history long enough to show seasons. The design holds 13 months of 64 channels across
225 cars, tabular and graphical, which forces tiered retention to keep the storage curve inside the contract's

5 percent annual escalation cap.
The fourth goal is hardware that survives the car. The electronics class is EN 50155 and IEC 60571 railway
electronics with IEC 61373 body-mounted shock and vibration, inside an 8x8x8-inch, IP62, 30-year-
corrosion, -10 to 170 degree F, 24 to 48 VDC battery envelope, with materials tightened to CFR 238 and the
USDOT recommended fire-safety practices. Three prototype cars carry the class before the 222-car rollout
begins.

Scoping decisions that de-risked the design
Three decisions taken early removed the risks that most often break a build of this shape, and each one cost
something we accepted deliberately.
The first was to ride the car system's cellular routers that already exist on every car, rather than design new
connectivity. This is the only path between the module and the cloud, so the telemetry design is built around
its NAT and port-forwarding behaviour from the start. The cost is that coverage on a moving fleet is
intermittent, so the design must carry store-and-forward buffering sized to the longest expected coverage
gap, with message queue depth monitored as a first-class metric. New connectivity would have bought
cleaner networking at the price of a fleet-wide installation we do not control.
The second was to execute the operator's own fault-logic table verbatim instead of building a learned fault
model. The table is named, the signals are named, and the mechanical desk already works in those terms. The
cost is that detection is bounded by the 64 named signals, and anomalies outside that vocabulary surface
only through the analog trending layer rather than through named logic.
The third was to specify the electronics as a class, EN 50155 and IEC 60571 with IEC 61373 vibration and CFR
238 fire materials, proven through type-test reports, rather than name part numbers. The cost is that
component selection sits with the contractor, and we audit the class rather than the box. The gain is schedule:
the 222-car rollout depends on shop access and car-house windows, and a class specification lets installation
proceed per window without waiting on a single part.

What we chose against
Every layer of this design had a competing option on the table, and the reasons for setting each aside are
specific to this operation rather than general preferences. Some were set aside on licence terms, some on fit
against what the requirement actually states, and some on the shape of the deployment itself. The table
below carries the decisions and their replacements, so we will not repeat its rows here.
Two exclusions deserve prose because they look like gaps and are not. First, no interface is built to train
control or PTC. The stock is FRA-regulated commuter equipment, and the monitoring system reads condition
data only, so keeping the two worlds separate keeps the certification boundary clean. Second, no on-site

server, data diode or air-gap layer is designed. Compute is contractor-hosted in the United States, the
telemetry rides the operator's existing cellular routers, and role-based accounts with MFA are the primary
control surface, so the one-way transfer stack answers to a requirement this design does not have. Likewise
no CMMS integration and no site server appear, because the requirement names neither. A design that
answers layers the requirement does not ask for pays for them in certification, cost and surface area, and
none of that cost buys this operator a visible fault any sooner.

Car to cloud through one fleet ontology
The system reads as one stack, and Figure 3 shows every component of it top to bottom: the surfaces the
operator's people open, the agents and the loop, the models and inference, the system of context, and the
ingestion tier underneath. Figure 4 shows the same stack as layers: one named source, the monitoring module
reading the 64 named train signals, feeds one adapter family that maps each reading into an ontology core of
14 objects, from car and input channel through active fault, fault history record, alert notification and slippery
rail hotspot, and that core grounds five services and three surfaces.
The flow runs upward. The module conditions the raw analogs, executes the operator's own fault-logic table,
and streams through the existing cellular routers on each car into contractor-hosted cloud ingestion, built to
the ClickHouse Cloud Architecture for Real Time Analytics pattern and substituted with self-managed open
source the operator owns. On the core sit the real-time dashboards, the 13-month history, and severity-
routed email and text alerting. Amazon Chronos-2, an Apache-2.0 licensed zero-shot forecasting model at
120M parameters, trends the analog channels with no fine tuning, and its residuals threshold into the alert
queue. Above that, the agentic work surface runs on Mistral Large 3 675B Instruct, self-hosted under

Apache-2.0, improving through memory rather than training. Hosting is contractor cloud in the United States
with Keycloak providing role-based accounts and MFA.

overtemperature fault at a site, from the reading that carries it to the mechanical desk controller dispatched
and the outcome written back to the ledger.

The fleet ontology
The centre of the design is not a document store but an ontology: fourteen object types that together are the
fleet. The plan puts the operator's car, the monitoring module, the car system, the digital input channel, the
analog input channel, the active fault, the fault history record, the alert notification, the mechanical desk
controller, the yard employee, the control centre, the office, the slippery rail hotspot and the notification
recipient group into one owned model, and every reading, fault and notification becomes a typed object linked
to the car it came from and the people who must act on it. This follows System of Context, published by
CodeNinja, which is the primary pattern the design stands on.
The typed links are what make the queries possible. A single query can reach from a smoothing reactor
overtemperature fault to the analog channel that produced it, to the car and its module, to the mechanical
desk controller responsible for that car's territory, and to the recipient group that gets the text. A document
store can hold the same records but cannot walk those edges, so every fleet-wide question becomes an
application-side join. The requirement demands subsecond fleet-wide active-fault views and tabular and
graphical history over 64 channels on 225 cars for 13 months, so the data layer adopts the ClickHouse Cloud
Architecture for Real Time Analytics, published by CLICKHOUSE, as its supporting pattern, with the managed
cloud service substituted by self-managed open source the operator owns.

component with the typed flows between layers and the hosting posture underneath, data residency in the

Ingestion and the event backbone
There is exactly one named source system in this build, the operator's own cellular that already rides on each
car for connectivity, and the telemetry design is built around its behaviour rather than around new

connectivity. The module speaks to the car system over the car's existing ethernet, GPS rides the same path,
and the requirement is explicit that this is the only path between the module and the cloud. The design
therefore assumes intermittent coverage from moving cars and treats it as normal operating condition, not as
an exception.
The adapter tier maps the operator's stream into the object model, and it is responsible for three things:
conditioning the raw analog signals before they become object events, carrying the per-channel calibration
recorded at prototype commissioning so every trend carries its provenance, and stamping each reading onto
the car, channel and fault objects it belongs to. Downstream, the streaming layer is responsible for delivery
through coverage gaps. Each module runs store-and-forward buffering sized to the longest expected
coverage gap at the agreed sample rate, and the message queue depth is monitored as a first-class metric
with a staleness alert route covering the rest. Figure 7 shows how data moves, each named source into the
adapter family that maps it, the adapters into the one ontology core, and the core out to the surfaces a person
opens.
Figure 8 shows the integration map, the one named system this build integrates with mapped through one
adapter family, each row carrying its provenance class. Because the source is the operator's own and its
behaviour is documented in the requirement, the adapter is specified against its NAT and port-forwarding
behaviour rather than discovered during commissioning, which is the guarantee the design can make at that
hop.

Figure 7:   How data moves: each named source into the adapter family that maps it, the adapters into the
one ontology core, the core out to the surfaces a person opens.

Figure 8:     The 1 named systems this build integrates with, mapped through 1 adapter family, each row
carrying its provenance class.

Inference and the edge
The first inference point is the module itself. The requirement supplies its own fault-logic table over 64 named
train signals, 32 digital and 32 analog, and the design executes that table rather than inventing a model
around it. The module is specified as a class, not a part number: EN 50155 and IEC 60571 railway electronics
with IEC 61373 body-mounted shock and vibration, EN 45545 to 2-class fire materials tightened by the
requirement to CFR 238 plus the USDOT recommended practices, inside an 8 by 8 by 8 inch, IP62, 30-year-
corrosion, -10 to 170 degree F, 24 to 48 VDC vehicle-battery envelope. Fault logic runs at the car so a fault
exists as an object even when the cellular link is not there, and only conditioned readings and active faults
cross the network boundary.
Four cameras complete the sensing half, aerial over the yard, wide at two sites, and aerial on a route segment,
watching for dynamic brake failure, smoothing reactor overtemperature, locked axle, motor current
imbalance, wheel slip and slide, slippery rail hotspots, MA frequency drift and hard coupling. Detections
resolve onto fleet objects in the event stream, and the latency budget for the desk-facing view is subsecond,
taken from the requirement's fleet-wide active-fault demand.
Figure 9 shows the hero workflow end to end: a smoothing reactor overtemperature fault at a site, from the
reading that carries it to the mechanical desk controller dispatched and the recovery written back to the
ledger, nothing waiting for a phone call. Figure 10 shows the camera wall at the moment of that event, four
feeds with the detections drawn on them. When the link drops, the module buffers and forwards, and the
staleness alert route tells the desk the feed is old rather than letting it look live.

Figure 9:    The hero workflow end to end: smoothing reactor overtemperature fault at the site, from the
reading that carries it to the recovery written back to the ledger.

Figure 10:     The camera wall at the moment of the event, smoothing reactor overtemperature fault at the
site: four feeds with the detections drawn on them, the event stream resolving each one onto the object
model, and active faults across the fleet on the excursion in faults.

Two models, both Apache-licensed
Two models are named in this design and both carry the Apache-2.0 licence, which is a design constraint here
and not a footnote. The System of Context rule is that nothing is trained for this customer, so the licence and
the no-training rule together decide what qualifies. The plan put GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3 aside specifically on
bespoke licence terms.
For the agentic work surface and ontology maintenance, the design runs Mistral Large 3 675B Instruct in FP8,
self-hosted on a single 141 GB HBM GPU class node and served with vLLM. The agents work over the fleet
ontology, read fault and condition data, and improve through memory rather than through training, which is
what the requirement's intake asks for explicitly. For the analog half, the design runs Amazon Chronos-2 for
anomaly detection and seasonal trending over the motor currents, thermocouples, accelerometers and speed
sensors. It is a 120M parameter model doing zero-shot forecasting across univariate, multivariate and
covariate channels with no fine tuning, which is what fits the no-training rule, and its residuals are thresholded
into the alert queue and feed the 13-month seasonal view the requirement asks for. At that size it trends 64
channels across 225 cars on modest hardware.
Figure 11 shows the three-layer stack the models sit in, with inference above the ontology and the surfaces
above that. The table below carries the full set of model choices with their roles and licences, so the rows are

not repeated here.

                                                 source the customer owns.

What degrades, and what must not
Each failure mode in this design has a stated answer, and the distinction the design draws is between what
degrades and what must not. The network fails first: coverage gaps on a moving 225-car fleet drop or delay
telemetry, so faults in a gap arrive late, and the design degrades to store-and-forward buffering sized to the
longest expected gap, with queue depth monitored and a staleness alert route. What must not degrade is the
module's own fault logic, which runs at the car on vehicle battery power, 24 to 48 VDC, so an active fault
exists before any link is needed.
The sensing can silently fail: the 64 signals are raw and a mis-scaled thermocouple or accelerometer poisons
every trend built on it, so the plan would bench-measure and calibrate every conditioned channel against
known references during prototype commissioning and record per-channel calibration in the system as
provenance. What must not degrade is the provenance itself, because a trend without it is unverifiable. The
source system can change under the design, and the adapter tier carries that risk, which is why its behaviour
is specified from the requirement rather than assumed. A model that stops being confident is answered by the
no-training rule: Chronos-2 residuals either cross the threshold into the alert queue or they do not, and the
alert budget with the desk during the 6-month tuning phase retires classes that produce no action, the
contractual hook being the requirement's own nuisance-fault elimination clause. The East Palestine
precedent, where a desk stopped treating a stream it could not act on, is the reason acknowledgement
tracking is per alert.
The contractor-hosted cloud is its own failure mode: if the service ends, the fault history, ontology and agent
context leave with it, so the plan would rehearse a full export during phase one and make data return and
deletion an explicit contract term. The table below carries the full set of failure modes and mitigations.

How the design was reasoned
The method started with the requirement read verbatim. The two sections were read in full, and the decision
that shaped most of the rest came from one of them: the requirement names its own 64 signals and its own
fault-logic table, so the design executes that table instead of inventing a model around it. The model choices
were then checked live against licence terms, which set aside two candidates and confirmed Mistral Large 3
675B and Chronos-2 on Apache-2.0.
For prior work, the design leans on the East Palestine case study for the alert-obligation rule, that every tier
names who acts, when and with what authority, and on the Deutsche Bahn switch case for environmental-
qualification-first sequencing, which is why the hardware half is written as a class specification before any
component choice. Samsara's DHL consolidation guided the one-stream-many-views shape without its
closed SaaS form. Two published patterns were adopted: System of Context as the primary, ClickHouse Cloud
Architecture for Real Time Analytics as the supporting data layer. One reference architecture, the AKS
Baseline Cluster Architecture, was proposed and set aside because its justification, read against the ask in
full, argued from nothing this operator stated. The proven shelf came back honestly empty: nothing in it
genuinely bears on rail fleet condition monitoring, and the treasury and defence-logistics precedents would
have been stretched repairs.
Figure 12 shows the reasoning end to end, the ask, the industry it resolved to, every research lens with what it
could see and what it cited. Three lenses came back with nothing usable, and the table below lists them: the
regulation lens was listed but no entry was read in full, the history lens held 63 rail entries none of which were
read this run, and the requirement states no sovereignty posture, so nothing in the design assumes one.

Evaluation and rollout
Nothing has been measured, so what follows is what the plan would measure. The headline measure is active
faults across the fleet, counted in faults, with the smoothing reactor overtemperature fault as the named
excursion and a breach declared when the count rises above its nominal level of zero. The staged workflow
the figures carry runs from the control centre to a site unattended, through a smoothing reactor
overtemperature fault at that site, to a mechanical desk controller dispatched, to the site settled and sealed in
the ledger with every asset audited. Figure 13 shows the coverage matrix, how the requirement's demands
map onto the components that answer them, which is the gate the design would be read against before any
phase closes.
The rollout runs in three phases with a gate at the end of each. Phase 1 is the prototype on 3 cars, carrying 12
items, and its gate is concrete: bench-measured calibration on every conditioned channel, a rehearsed full
export of the ontology, fault history and agent memory, and a full module installation rehearsed off-car before
the first car. Phase 2 is the fleet rollout across the remaining 222 cars, carrying 4 items, and its schedule is
built from the operator's available installation windows per car house rather than from the software plan,
because shop access is the constraint that broke comparable programmes and the contractor does not
control it. Phase 3 is service operations, carrying 1 item, and its gate is the alert budget agreed with the desk
after the 6-month tuning phase, with alert classes that produced no action retired under the nuisance-fault
elimination clause.
Figure 14 shows the delivery timeline across the three phases. The design also prices the 13-month retention
curve, full-resolution recent data over downsampled seasonal history, into the service contract before
signature, against the requirement's 5 percent annual escalation cap.

Figure 13:    Coverage matrix for a predictive maintenance rolling stock design, matching each requirement
in the operator's ask to the component of the system that answers it.

Figure 14:   Delivery timeline for a rail fleet condition monitoring system rollout, running from the three car
prototype phase through fleet rollout on 222 cars to service operations.

Lessons learned
The lessons from this design fall into two groups, one about building the fleet ontology before the agents that
read it, and one about treating the railway's own constraints, coverage gaps, shop windows and alert fatigue,

as design rather than operational afterthoughts. Each is set out below with the decision that produced it.
Execute the customer's fault table, do not invent a model
The requirement named 32 digital and 32 analog signals per car and carried its own fault-logic table in its own
section. We designed the modules and the alert pipeline to execute that table verbatim rather than wrapping it
in a learned model, because the operator's mechanical desk already knows what each fault means and has to
act on it.
Licence terms eliminate models before benchmarks do
We set aside two otherwise strong candidates on bespoke licence terms before any performance comparison,
and committed to Mistral Large 3 675B Instruct and Amazon Chronos-2, both Apache-2.0. Check the licence
first, because a model you cannot self-host under acceptable terms is not a candidate no matter how it
benchmarks.
Qualify the hardware class before designing the electronics
The electronics class governs the whole hardware half: EN 50155 and IEC 60571 railway electronics, IEC
61373 shock and vibration, CFR 238 fire materials, all inside the operator's 8x8x8-inch IP62 battery-powered
envelope. We sequenced the environmental qualification first so no board decision could be made that the
class would later reverse.
Route alerts by severity or the stream gets ignored
The East Palestine case study carried the lesson that an alert nobody treats seriously is worse than no alert.
We budgeted the email and text stream with the desk during a 6-month tuning phase, routed by severity with
acknowledgement tracking, and wrote a nuisance-fault elimination clause into the scope as the contractual
hook for retiring alert classes that produce no action.
Size the buffer for the coverage gap you will actually get
Telemetry rides the operator's existing cellular routers on moving cars, so intermittent coverage is the design
condition, not an edge case. We specified store-and-forward buffering sized to the longest expected
coverage gap at the agreed sample rate, with queue depth monitored as a first-class metric and a staleness
alert route behind it.

What is still open
Three questions could not be closed from the requirement, and each would change the design if settled. The
sovereignty posture is not stated anywhere in the requirement, so nothing in this design assumes one; settling
it would decide whether contractor-hosted compute in the United States stands or whether a data boundary
layer has to be added. The regulation lens was listed but no entry was read in full during this run, so the

regulatory touchpoints, CFR 238 and the USDOT recommended fire-safety practices, are named from the
requirement itself; reading the lens properly could tighten the materials specification or add touchpoints the
requirement does not name. The history lens held 63 rail entries, none of which were read this run, so the East
Palestine case study carries the historical argument alone; reading the wider rail record could surface
precedents for the rollout scheduling risk that the current mitigation handles from a single case.
A fourth question is contractual rather than technical: the 13-month retention of 64 channels across 225 cars
against the 5 percent annual escalation cap depends on a storage curve that has to be priced into the service
contract before signature. The table below carries the full set of open questions and what each one would
change.

Conclusion
The design is a rail fleet condition monitoring system for a rail and transportation operator in the United
States, built as three layers that each do one job. Monitoring modules on a 225-car commuter fleet read 64
named signals and execute the operator's own fault-logic table at the car, on EN 50155-class electronics
inside an IP62, vehicle-battery-powered envelope, tested on 3 prototype cars before the 222-car rollout.
Telemetry rides the cellular routers already on each car into a contractor-hosted US cloud, where a 14-object
fleet ontology grounds real-time dashboards, severity-routed email and text alerting, and 13 months of
history. On top sits the agent work surface: Mistral Large 3 675B and Chronos-2, both Apache-licensed, self-
hosted, improving through memory rather than training.
Running it somewhere else means three substitutions. The hardware half is already a class specification
rather than a bill of materials, so the electronics envelope transfers as written. The models are self-hosted on

open licences, so the inference layer moves with the operator, and the data layer is self-managed open source
for the same reason. What does not transfer is the operator's own fault-logic table and the cellular behaviour
the adapter is specified against; a new fleet brings its own signal names, its own fault table and its own
connectivity, and the adapter tier is where that work happens.

title: Warehouse Twin Command: Live Slotting, Docks, Yards and Safety Vision for Warehousing and Intralogistics in the United States
text:
V E R T I C A L - D R I V E N A R C H I T E C T U R E S · WA R E H O U S I N G & I N T R A L O G I S T I C S · D E S I G N E D W I T H P R A X I S ·
OCTOBER 2026

Warehouse Twin Command: Live
Slotting, Docks, Yards and Safety Vision
for Every Site
A live digital twin of the four United States sites of a warehousing and intralogistics operator,
built from warehouse, labor and yard data, that produces weekly slotting recommendations,
dock and yard schedules and on-site safety vision, with every action drafted for a person to
approve.

CodeNinja Engineering Team

For the network operations director, site and safety managers, and the data, platform, ontology and vision engineers
who would build and run it.

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-
world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for
designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

ABSTRACT

A Near Miss Should Be Data, Not Paper
The operation needs one question answered continuously across its four sites in the United States: where
every trailer, slot, task and person is right now, and what should change next, from the door a carrier
should back into, to the slot a fast-moving SKU should occupy and the walking a move would save, to the
forklift and pedestrian near misses that occurred on today's shift and never reached anyone. No system
the operation runs can answer it. The warehouse management system holds locations, inventory and pick
paths but not labor, carriers or video; the labor system holds hours and rates but not the floor; the yard
lives in a spreadsheet that is stale by mid-shift; roughly 220 cameras record for security and no one
reviews them; and near misses are captured on paper, if at all. The documented cost of the failure is
severe, because forklift and pedestrian incidents in warehousing are frequent and often serious or fatal
(Cisco-eagle n.d.; OSHA 2023).

The design builds a live digital twin of each site as a system of context: an ontology of fourteen objects
projected over five source systems through one adapter family, kept true by nightly reconciliation against
the warehouse management system, which remains the system of record. Six services run on that model,
from the live building twin, slotting intelligence and dock and yard scheduling to edge safety vision,
platform and sovereignty, and the site manager assistant, and they reach people through four surfaces: a
floor console for safety alarms, a clip review and coaching queue, the assistant work surface, and safety
analytics. Safety vision processes the existing camera estate at each site on an industrial edge server
with one 48 GB inference card, so only events and short clips leave the building, and no face recognition
or re-identification runs anywhere. Five open-weight models carry the work: RF-DETR detection and OC-
SORT tracking on the site edge GPU, a 27B dense model for assistant continuity when the wide area link
drops, an embedding model for retrieval over records and procedures, and a 675B frontier assistant on
one node of the company's own hardware, all under Apache-2.0 or MIT terms the operator holds outright.

The paper covers the industry problem and the join failure between existing systems, the constraints that
fix where everything runs, the layered stack, the fourteen-object model and its typed links, ingestion
through the adapter tier, the placement of inference across the edge, the site and the center, the five
models and their licenses, the two-phase rollout with its item counts and exit gates, ownership of what the
system builds, and finally how Praxis contextualized and reasoned the design.

  Figure 1. Warehouse Twin Command on one page: the sources the operation already runs, one object model, what it
                                      computes, and the person who decides.

         Sources                                                               Reference

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

A Forklift Near Miss Never Becomes Data

Forklift and pedestrian incidents in warehousing are frequent, documented and often serious,
yet the operation learns about them from paper after the fact, because no system it runs
holds the building together.

The abstract promised a live digital twin of four buildings, built from data the operation already holds, with
safety vision on cameras that already exist. This chapter states the question that twin exists to answer,
what the absence of an answer costs when forklifts and pedestrians share a floor, and the scenario the
design must fit without replacing anything.

1.1 The Question, the Data and the Rules

The question the operation needs answered is a daily one: where in each building is work unsafe or
inefficient right now, and what single change this week would improve it. Answering it requires data no
one system holds: the locations, inventory, open orders and pick paths of the warehouse management
system; the shifts, zones and hours of the labor system; the trailers, carriers and appointments of the
yard; and the continuous visual record of the cameras over docks, aisles and yards. It must satisfy the
powered industrial truck standard, OSHA 1910.178, which governs forklift operation and operator
evaluation, and the operator's own rule that associates' privacy is respected with no face recognition
anywhere in the system. The ask also names open weights in the company's own environment, which
places the regulatory ground alongside a sovereignty commitment.

1.2 The Documented Cost

The cost of the problem is documented and severe. Pedestrians suffer 26 percent of all forklift related
injuries, and these injuries are often serious or fatal (Cisco-eagle n.d.). The fatality record shows the
pattern repeating across jurisdictions: a lumber mill employee in Oregon died after being struck by a
forklift (OHSU 2023); a major freight distribution company appeared in court after a forklift incident left a
man fatally injured (GOVT 2018); and a potato producer was fined 180,000 dollars after a worker was
seriously injured by a reversing forklift (SA 2025). The United States safety regulator has responded with
a Regional Emphasis Program for powered industrial vehicles and warehousing operations, which raises
inspection attention on exactly this hazard class (OSHA 2023). Each of these events was discovered after
the fact. None of them became data at the moment they happened, which is the failure this design
addresses.

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

The scenario is a warehousing and intralogistics operator in the United States running four distribution
centers. Each building has dock doors, racked storage aisles, a yard for trailers, and a shift-based
workforce of associates, shift leads and a site manager; a supervisor reviews safety matters and a safety
lead owns the program. About 220 fixed cameras across the estate already cover the docks, aisles and
yards for security and record to a video management system. The operation runs five named systems: a
warehouse management system, a labor management system, a yard management spreadsheet, the
video management system and a carrier appointment source. The physical environments are the dock
edge, where trailers meet doors and people; the aisle ends, where forklifts and pedestrians cross; and the
yard, where trailers dwell and hostlers move. The regulatory ground is the powered industrial truck

standard, state labor rules, and the operator's stated privacy rule. Four places, five systems, one building
per site that no system holds whole.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 2

Every System Sees One Slice of the Building

The warehouse management system, the labor system, the yard spreadsheet and the video
estate each hold one true slice of the operation, and none of them can answer the questions
that cross the slices.

Chapter 1 stated the question and the cost of leaving it unanswered. This chapter shows why no system
the operator already runs can answer it: each holds one true slice of the building, and the questions that
matter cross the slices.

2.1 What Each System Sees

The warehouse management system is the truth source for the building: locations, inventory, open orders,
pick tasks and dock doors. What it misses is the physical world those records describe: it does not know
who is standing at the aisle end, how fast a truck took the corner, or whether the exit the pick path relies
on is blocked. The labor management system sees shifts, headcount by zone, hours and units per hour. It
misses where the work physically happened and every hazard on the floor, because it records labor as
numbers, not as movement. The yard management spreadsheet sees trailers, carriers and yard slots as
they were last typed. It misses live dwell time, door state and arrival reality, and it depends on someone
remembering to update it. The video management system sees everything: every dock, aisle and yard,
recorded continuously. It misses meaning, because a recording is not a detection, an event or an alert,
and no camera view is linked to an order, a shift or a slot. The carrier appointment source sees booked
appointments and carriers. It misses arrival actuals, unload progress and which door a trailer should take.
Figure 2 sets these five systems side by side, each sees column honest and each misses column
decisive.

     Figure 2. Five systems, each seeing one part of the answer. The question needs all of them in one place at once.

2.2 What None of Them See Together

The questions that matter need all five slices at once, and no join exists. Which slotting move saves the
most walking needs pick tasks, slot locations and SKU velocity together with labor by zone. Which door a
trailer should take needs appointments, live unload rates and labor on shift. Whether an aisle end is
dangerous needs the camera view, the shift schedule and the pick path that sends people through it.
Today those answers are assembled by people, from a spreadsheet, a screen and a walk down the floor,
which is why a near miss at an aisle crossing produces a paper report weeks later or nothing at all. The
cost in practice is threefold: safety learning arrives after the fact, slotting decisions run on stale velocity,
and carrier wait time is invisible until a carrier complains. The design's object model is the join these
systems never had.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 3

Four Rules Fix Where Everything Runs

Video processed at each site, no face recognition, safety functions left with certified
equipment, and open weights in the company's own environment: these four rules settle the
placement of every component downstream.

Chapter 2 showed that the join failure is structural: five systems, five slices, no shared model. The design
could repair that join in many shapes, and four rules from the operator's own requirement settle which

shape survives: where video runs, what vision may never do, who keeps the safety function, and whose
environment the weights live in.

3.1 Video Is Processed at Each Site

The first rule is that video is processed at each site, and only events and short clips leave the building.
This is hard in warehousing because the camera estate is large, about 220 fixed cameras, and the
tempting architecture is a cloud analytics service that ingests every stream. That path is closed twice
over: it moves raw video across the wide area link, and it puts the detection weights in someone else's
environment. The rule forces inference onto an edge server at each distribution center, sized from the
measured decode and inference budget on the camera substreams, with the one-way egress path made
a physical property rather than a configuration promise.

3.2 No Face Recognition, No Re-identification

The second rule is that associates' privacy is respected and no face recognition runs anywhere. This is
hard because safety vision watches people by design, and the easiest way to make tracking robust is a
re-identification branch that learns what a person looks like. The design holds the line structurally: the
tracker is motion-only, with no appearance model, so a detection is a moving object in a zone and never a
named individual. The payoff is adoption as much as compliance, because a safety system the floor
reads as surveillance stops being told anything.

3.3 Analytics Advise, Certified Equipment Stops

The third rule is that camera analytics are an operational feedback loop, never a safety-rated stop. The
powered industrial truck standard already assigns safety functions to certified equipment and trained
operators, and nothing in this design takes one over: no autonomous control of forklifts, doors or any
equipment. This is hard because the vision system will sometimes see a hazard a person misses, and the
urge to act directly is strong. The design answers with people deciding coaching: every safety event
becomes a clip a supervisor reviews, and the machine's job is to capture the near miss that paper never
caught.

3.4 Open Weights in the Company's Own Environment

The fourth rule is that data and models stay in the company's own environment, on open weights. This is
hard at the scale the assistant needs: the frontier-class work surface model carries hundreds of billions of
parameters, and hosting it in-country on operator hardware rules out the hosted API that would otherwise
be the simple answer. Every model in the stack therefore carries a license the operator can hold outright,

One Stack Reaches From Records to the Floor

A layered stack runs from the five systems of record, through one adapter family and an

Chapter 3 settled the constraints: the systems of record stay, data stays inside the company's

4.1 A Three-Tier Pattern and Why It Fits

The pattern is three tiers. Below sit the five systems of record: the warehouse management system, the
labor management system, the yard management spreadsheet, the video management system and the
carrier appointment source. In the middle sits one object model, held in an ontology store on the
operator's own hardware, that projects those records as fourteen objects with typed links and stays true
by reconciling against them rather than by becoming a record itself. Above sit the applications and
agents: six services that reason over the twin and four surfaces that people actually use. Nothing above
the middle tier writes a source system, and nothing below the middle tier is replaced except the yard
spreadsheet, which the dock and yard scheduling module retires.

This shape fits the operation for three reasons. The warehouse management system keeps its position as
the system of record, so the twin never competes with it for truth. Safety vision runs at each site on the
existing camera estate of roughly 220 fixed IP cameras, so video is processed in the building and only

events and short clips ever leave it. And the same ontology serves slotting, dock and yard scheduling,
safety and the site manager assistant, so each capability strengthens the others instead of building its
own data island. Figure 3 shows the layered stack with the count at each layer: five sources, one adapter
family, fourteen objects, six services and four surfaces.

5.1 Fourteen Objects and Their Typed Links

Fourteen objects carry the whole twin. Distribution Center is anchored in the WMS site master and holds
each building's square footage, dock door count, shift pattern, camera count and WAN link. Dock Door
and Yard Trailer are anchored in the yard management spreadsheet until the new dock and yard module

takes over as the yard system of record. Storage Slot, SKU, Open Order and Pick Task are anchored in
the WMS. Associate and Labor Shift are anchored in the labor management system. Camera Zone is
anchored in the video management system. Safety Event digitizes what paper near-miss reports hold

The typed links are what make this an argument rather than an archive, and Figure 4 draws all of them. A
query can start at a Yard Trailer, walk to the Dock Door it is staged at, on to the SKUs whose travel
distance from dock is measured, to the Pick Tasks those SKUs feed, to the Associate each task is
assigned to, and finish at the Shift Lead who owns that associate's shift: one traversal from a trailer in the
yard to the labor it will consume and the person accountable for it. A document store holds each of those
records as a separate document, so the same question needs a hand-written join at every hop, and the
slotting service, the dock scheduler and the assistant each rebuild the same joins privately. Here the joins
are declared once, and every service reads the same ones.

Five Systems Feed the Twin Through One Gate

Every source enters through the adapter tier, never directly, so the twin's picture can be
reconciled against the systems of record it projects and drift is caught the same day.

Chapter 5 showed what the object model holds. This chapter covers how data reaches it: five named
sources, one adapter family, and an event backbone that keeps order even when the wide area link does
not.

6.1 Five Sources and Their Provenance

Figure 5 maps the five sources and their provenance classes. Four are confirmed at intake as the
operator's own systems, all read-only to the design: the warehouse management system, the twin's truth
source for locations, inventory, open orders and pick tasks; the labor management system, feeding
associates and labor shifts as well as the live unload rates dock scheduling leans on; the yard
management spreadsheet, imported once and then retired as the dock and yard module becomes the
yard system of record; and the video management system, whose roughly 220 recorded cameras the
safety vision rides rather than replaces. The fifth, the carrier appointment source, is domain-typical: the
requirement names appointments but not the system behind them, so a class-typical booking feed enters
through the same adapter with its provenance marked, and every downstream consumer can see which
facts rest on an assumed source until the operator names the real one.

          Figure 5. The 5 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

6.2 What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

One adapter family, the integration adapter, stands between every source and the ontology, and it
guarantees four things. Every object carries provenance: the source system, the timestamp and the offset
it came from, so any figure on any surface traces back to its record. Every write is an idempotent upsert
keyed on the natural identifier, so a replayed stream cannot duplicate a trailer or a pick task. Every unit
and coordinate is normalized on the way in: aisle, bay and level for slots, meters per second for calibrated
speeds. And every night the adapter tier counts objects against the systems of record and surfaces drift
the same day, which is what keeps a projection honest. The warehouse management system stays read-
only throughout; the only system the design replaces is the yard spreadsheet.

6.3 The Event Backbone

Apache Kafka 4.3, in KRaft mode, is the backbone. Ordering is per key: events for one dock door, one
SKU or one camera zone land on one partition and keep their order, and linuxptp with chrony keeps
camera clocks and server clocks close enough that a forklift event and a WMS event order correctly
against each other. Delivery is at-least-once into idempotent consumers, so nothing is lost to a restart.
Buffering is sized for the survival window at the measured event and clip rate, then doubled, so a wide
area outage longer than expected drops nothing: events and clips accumulate on site storage and flow
when the link returns. Replication covers the central aggregation across the four sites, Harbor carries the
air-gapped artifact and model registry, InfluxDB 3 Core holds telemetry, and Prometheus, Grafana and
Loki observe the whole path, so the backbone's own health is as visible as the site's.

Detection Belongs at the Edge and Reasoning in House

Detection and tracking run on a site edge server so only events and short clips leave the
building, the site keeps a degraded-mode assistant on its own card, and the frontier weights
run on the company's own central hardware.

Chapter 6 described how five source systems enter through adapters and land in the object model as
events. This chapter decides where the intelligence that reads those events runs: which models sit beside
the cameras, which sit beside the associates, and which sit on the company's own central hardware.

7.1 Three Tiers, Each with a Reason

The design places inference at three tiers, and Figure 6 shows all of them together: the edge tier on each
site's rack server, the site tier on the same box, and the central tier in the operator's own environment.
The edge tier carries the vision stack: RF-DETR detection checkpoints watching forklifts, order pickers,
pedestrians, vests, pallets and trailers on the camera substreams, OC-SORT associating detections into
tracks so one event becomes one alert rather than ten, and the zone rules that turn a track into a
proximity, speeding or blocked-exit event. Detection belongs here because the constraint is explicit: video
is processed at each site, and only events and short clips leave the building. The site tier carries
Qwen3.8-27B, whose FP8 weights are about 31 GB and fit one 48 GB PCIe inference card with
headroom for its KV cache, so the site manager assistant keeps answering when the wide area link
drops, alongside BGE-M3 for embedding retrieval over safety records and procedures at about 1.1 GB in
FP16. The central tier carries Mistral Large 3 675B, the frontier work surface model, on one node of the
141 GB HBM class: eight cards give about 1,038 GB of usable memory at 0.92 utilization, the FP8
weights published at about 682 GB fit inside it, and roughly 350 GB of KV ceiling remains for concurrent
assistant sessions across the estate. The arithmetic is the argument: each tier's weights, usable memory
and KV ceiling were checked before anything else about the tier was decided, because a model that does
not fit is not a placement choice.

           Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.

7.2 The Latency Budget

The budget follows the two-clocks rule the design set in its first principles: milliseconds on the truck,
seconds in orchestration. The safety path is the tight one. A pedestrian stepping into an aisle end must be
detected, tracked and raised as an alarm to the shift lead's live floor console within the time a person can
still act, which is why detection and tracking run on the edge GPU next to the cameras rather than round
a wide area link. Temporal confirmation on event tubes trades a small amount of that time for precision,
because an alarm the floor learns to ignore is worse than no alarm at all; the alert budget is set before
thresholds, and per-camera dismissal trends are watched weekly. The assistant path runs on the seconds
clock: a site manager asks the twin a question, retrieval over the ontology and BGE-M3 embeddings
assembles the context, and the model answers in conversational time. Slotting intelligence has no latency
pressure at all and runs weekly against reconciled data, which is why it reads the twin rather than the raw
streams.

7.3 What Crosses the Boundary, and What Fails

Only two things cross the site boundary: safety events with short clips, and the telemetry and twin
aggregates the central tier reads. The events-and-clips path can be hardened with a hardware-enforced
one-way egress option, which makes "only events and short clips leave the building" a physical property
rather than a configuration promise; lidi and Eurydice are the verified transfer software beside the diode.
When the wide area link fails, the site does not stop: detection, tracking, the live floor console and the
degraded-mode assistant on the 27B card all continue locally, and a store-and-forward buffer sized for the
survival window at the measured event and clip rate, then doubled, holds everything until the link returns;
the longest historical outage at each site is a discovery question, not an assumption. When power fails,
the edge node and its PoE switches ride one UPS, and Network UPS Tools v2.8.5 orders a clean
shutdown before the battery runs out, so the object model resynchronizes rather than corrupts. When the
update path is the failure, each site pulls container images and model weights from a Harbor registry
inside the operator's own environment, so an update that cannot reach a site leaves that site running its
last good versions rather than reaching for the internet. No failure in the link, the power or the update path
puts a camera stream outside the building.

licenses, with their triggers and attribution duties, drove the picks rather than convenience.

Chapter 7 placed each model at its tier and checked the memory arithmetic. This chapter examines the
licenses those models carry, because the requirement that data and models stay in the company's own
environment on open weights makes the license terms, not the benchmark scores, the deciding factor.
Figure 7 sets the five models out as one stack. The frontier tier is Mistral Large 3 675B, a 675 billion
parameter instruct model serving the agentic work surface and ontology maintenance: the site manager
assistant over the twin, and the surface the operator's own people build agents on. Its published FP8
checkpoint is about 682 GB, which its publisher states fits one node of eight 141 GB HBM class GPUs or
192 GB HBM class GPUs, while the NVFP4 build fits a node of 80 GB class cards. It runs centrally on the
operator's own hardware, and it is Apache-2.0: no revenue trigger, no attribution duty, so the operator
owns the weights outright. It was chosen over GLM 5.3, whose publisher is on the US Entity List, and
over Mistral-licensed neighbors whose revenue triggers would engage as the estate grows. The site tier is
Qwen3.8-27B, a dense Apache-2.0 model whose footprint is about 56 GB at 16 bit, about 28 GB at 8 bit
and about 14 GB at 4 bit, weights only, which is why one 48 GB PCIe card holds it at FP8 with KV
headroom for assistant continuity during WAN loss. It was picked from the small-on-site family for one-
card density and long context. The embedding model is BGE-M3, MIT licensed with an 8,192 token
window, so a whole standard operating procedure stays one passage; it produces dense, sparse and
multi-vector output from one pass, which keeps error codes and slot identifiers retrievable on a small box,

detection: the rfdetr package and its Nano to Large detection checkpoints are Apache-2.0, occupying
about 61 to 68 MB at 16 bit, and take site fine-tuning for evaluation sets; the XL and 2XL checkpoints in

the segmentation path and over YOLO26, whose AGPL gate is wrong for a system the operator owns.
Beside it runs OC-SORT for multi-object tracking: MIT licensed, motion-only, built for objects that turn and
stop unpredictably, which forklifts and pedestrians at aisle ends are, with association running at about 700
FPS on a CPU given detections. It has no re-identification branch, which keeps the privacy posture the
constraint sets, and it was picked over the Roboflow trackers collection for license minimalism on the hot
path. Together these choices answer the regulatory ground beneath them: the safety vision exists
because pedestrians suffer 26 percent of all forklift related injuries, often serious or fatal (Cisco-eagle
n.d.), and the US safety regulator's regional emphasis program on powered industrial vehicles and
warehousing operations shows where enforcement attention sits (OSHA 2023).

9.4 Lessons

Survey the cameras before trusting them. Cameras hung for human review of wide scenes rarely carry
the pixel density a model needs at an aisle end or a dock edge, so the six-gate survey is architecture, not
due diligence, and its recorded evidence is what makes the mixed-estate decision defensible.

Set the alert budget before the thresholds. Thresholds tuned to impress in a demo produce a floor that
stops reacting; fixing the budget first forces the design to earn its alerts, and the dismissal trend tells the
shift lead whether the budget holds.

Keep the review lane permanent. The case-study reading taught that the manual review queue is not
scaffolding to remove: it stays as the ground-truth source for accuracy measurement and threshold tuning
for the life of the system.

9.5 What Is Still Open

Four questions remain open. The measured behavior of the WMS event surface is unknown until the pilot
instruments it, and settling it sets how fresh the slotting velocity can be. The longest historical wide area
outage at each site is a discovery question, and its answer sizes the store-and-forward buffer that
protects events and clips. The camera reuse survey outcome decides how many purpose-placed fixed
cameras the mixed estate needs. The warehouse quota statutes of the four states decide which
anonymization options the review surfaces must carry. Each answer changes a number or a setting, not
the architecture.

10.1 What the Operator Holds

The object model is the operator's from the first day: the 14 objects and their typed links are anchored in
the operator's own systems of record, the WMS site and item masters, the labor system and the video
management system, so the twin is a projection the operator can inspect, extend and re-host rather than
a product it rents. The weights are the operator's because every model in the register carries Apache-2.0
or MIT terms with no revenue trigger and no attribution duty on the running system, held on the operator's
own hardware; the design improves through memory loops rather than fine-tunes, so there is no
production fine-tune to own, and the label sets, calibration files and threshold settings used for accuracy
measurement belong to the operator with the rest. The decision record is the operator's institutional
memory: every slotting approval with its stated walking saved, every coaching decision, every safety
event review outcome and every carrier wait measurement is kept as a record the next decision reads,
and it is memory, not a training signal. The boundary is the operator's ground: the site edge servers, the
camera segment, the untouched VMS recording path and the one-way egress that lets only events and
short clips leave the building, enforced as a physical property rather than a configuration promise.

10.2 The Offer Behind the Design

This design maps directly onto CodeNinja's offer. Adaptive Operations covers the sensing, detection and
forecasting of physical behavior: forklift and pedestrian proximity, speeding in pedestrian zones and
blocked exits on the existing camera estate, processed at each site. Decision Systems covers the
ranking, attribution, reconciliation and recommendations a named person decides: weekly slotting moves
that state the walking saved, door assignments from appointments and live unload rates, and the truth
reconciliation that keeps the twin honest against the WMS. Hyper Ontology is the object model itself, the
14 objects and their typed links. Hyper Pragma is the work surface where the operator's people build their
own agents over the twin, including the site manager assistant that drafts actions for a person to approve.
Hyper Engram is the kept record of decisions and outcomes that the next decision reads. Sovereign
Infrastructure is the posture the whole design rests on: the operator's own hardware, open-weight
licenses and in-country operation with only events and clips leaving each building. And Praxis is the
platform that produced this design, which is how a reader can trace every choice in it back to recorded
reading.

PA R T I V · C O N C L U S I O N

One Twin, Held by the People Who Run the Floors
In one view, the design is a system of context: a live twin of four sites projected over the systems of
record the operation already runs, reconciled nightly so it stays true, with safety vision processed inside
each building on the cameras already there, slotting and scheduling recommendations that state their
own cost before a person approves them, and an assistant that drafts actions and never decides them.
Nothing replaces a system of record except the yard spreadsheet the design retires, and nothing leaves a
building except events and short clips.

Running the same shape elsewhere takes three things: source systems that expose events an adapter
tier can read, a camera estate that survives a reuse survey covering access, density, angle, time
behavior, condition and worst-hour environment, and the discipline to hold every dependent capability
behind a pilot gate that measures realized walking saved, carrier wait time and alert acceptance against
baselines stated before the work starts. Where those hold, the pattern transfers: project, do not replace;
reconcile, do not trust; detect, never identify.

PA R T I V · C H A P T E R 11

Every Choice Traces Back to Recorded Reading

Every choice in this design traces to recorded reading on Praxis: the ask as stated, the
records read in full, and eight lenses that each left a mark on the architecture.

Chapter 10 established that the operator holds the object model, the weights, the decision record and the
boundary. This final chapter opens the record of how the design itself was produced, so that any choice
can be traced to what justified it (Figure 9). Every design in the Vertical-Driven Architectures series is
produced on Praxis, the platform for designing physical AI systems. This chapter lets a reader trace any
choice in this paper back to what justified it: the ask as stated, the records read in full, and eight lenses
that each left a mark on the architecture.

11.1 Contextualizing the Ask

The ask was stated in the operator's own words: a live digital twin of four United States distribution
centers built from the WMS, labor and yard data, with weekly slotting recommendations, dock and yard
scheduling, safety vision on the existing 220 cameras processed at each site, and a site manager
assistant that drafts actions for a person to approve, under OSHA 1910.178, with no face recognition and
open weights in the company's own environment. Praxis assigned the design to the system of context
family in the Warehousing and Intralogistics industry, in the United States by the operator's own
requirement. The room held the ask, the operator's intake answers, and three shelves read in full and

available on request: 18 case-study records, 455 tooling and recency records, and 29 hardware and
equipment records.

title: Pipeline Integrity Watch: Leak Detection, Fleet Health and Security Directive Evidence for Natural Gas Transmission in the United States
text:
VERTICAL-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURES · OIL & GAS · DESIGNED WITH PRAXIS · OCTOBER 2026

Pipeline Integrity Watch: Leak Detection,
Fleet Health and Security Directive
Evidence for Every Station
A single on-premises model of a United States natural gas transmission estate that passively
monitors the OT network, watches compressor health and leak indicators at every station,
and explains each alert to a controller who decides every action.

CodeNinja Engineering Team

For the vice president of operations and pipeline integrity, gas control and compliance managers, and the OT security,
reliability, data and platform engineers who would build and run it.

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-
world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on CodeNinja Praxis, the CodeNinja
Atoms platform for designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

ABSTRACT

The Evidence Should Generate Itself From the
Monitoring
A United States gas transmission operator needs four questions answered at once: is the line tight
tonight, is each compressor unit drifting from its healthy signature, is the OT network at every station
behaving as inventoried, and can the security directive evidence be shown on demand. Today those
questions live in separate systems that never meet, because the historian holds the process tags, the
alarm and event stream holds what controllers saw, the CMMS holds what maintenance did, and the
security posture lives in documents assembled by hand; a leak signature spread across pressure, flow,
methane and camera evidence arrives as unrelated alarms, and the evidence record is typed after the
fact rather than generated by the monitoring itself.

The design builds one living model of the pipeline estate on the operator's own hardware: four source
systems enter through three adapter families into an object model of fourteen objects; ten services run

across station edge nodes and the gas control centers; seven surfaces present the findings to controllers,
engineers and compliance owners; and four open-weight models carry the intelligence, with Chronos-2
forecasting and RF-DETR scene detection running on station edge hardware that keeps working through
backhaul loss, and Mistral Large 3 675B with BGE-M3 running beside them in the control center under
licenses the operator can hold outright. Passive taps watch the OT network, data diodes enforce one-way
passage out of station zones, the control room assistant explains each alert in plain words with the data
behind it and drafts a response, and a controller decides every action; the system never writes to a field
device.

Part I states the problem and the join failure across the estate's systems of record; Part II sets the
constraints, the stack, the object model, the adapter discipline, the placement of inference and the model
licenses; Part III carries the two-phase rollout with its gates, the failure modes, and ownership of what the
design builds; and Part IV closes with how Praxis contextualized and reasoned the design, so any choice
can be traced to what justified it.

    Figure 1. Pipeline Integrity Watch on one page: the sources the operation already runs, one object model, what it
                                        computes, and the person who decides.
