PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

Every Station Speaks, Nobody Joins the Sentences

A transmission estate continuously produces the evidence of leaks, failing compressors and
network intrusions, but it is scattered across systems that cannot be read together, so each
risk is discovered late and evidenced by hand.

The abstract promised a living model of the pipeline estate that watches, explains and drafts while a
person decides. Before that promise can be argued, the problem itself has to be stated precisely: what
the operation needs to know each day, why the systems it already owns cannot say it, and what the
regulatory regimes require it to prove.

1.1 The Question the Operation Needs Answered

A transmission estate asks the same four questions every hour, and each one is a join across data the
operation already holds. Is this pressure and flow deviation a leak, or line pack responding to a ramp? Is
this compressor unit drifting toward failure, or operating normally for its running hours? Is anyone
unexpected inside the operational technology network at a station? And can the operation prove, on
demand, that its security measures are in place and its alarm management plan is being followed?
Answering the first question needs one-second pressure and flow telemetry along the line plus meter
accuracy; the second needs vibration and discharge temperature joined to maintenance history; the third
needs passive network traffic from the stations; the fourth needs all of the above held as evidence. The
regimes that govern the answers are the United States pipeline safety rules under 49 CFR Part 192,
including the alarm management requirements of 192.631 and incident reporting under Part 191, the
computational pipeline monitoring practices of API RP 1130, and the transportation security directives that
apply to hazardous liquid and natural gas pipelines. The design encodes rule versions as objects rather
than hard-coding them, because the United States methane and pipeline leak rules changed status
repeatedly between 2024 and 2026.

1.2 The Documented Cost of the Problem

The cost of discovering a fault late, rather than reading its early signature, is documented in public
investigation records. A major United Kingdom energy company was fined after failing to properly
maintain pipework for seven years, a lapse that led to a major hydrocarbon release (HSE 2025). A loss of
primary containment at a United States liquefied natural gas facility traced back to instrument and
procedural failures that the investigation report set out in full (DOT 2022). In a prosecuted case, the wall
thickness of hydrocarbon-containing pipework deteriorated through a local corrosion mechanism until the
pipework failed (HSE n.d.). These are the tail of the distribution, but the mechanism is ordinary: the
evidence of deterioration exists in the data for a long time before anyone can read it, because it is
scattered. For this operator the recurring cost is not the rare catastrophe but the daily one, evidence
assembled by hand for every review, every audit and every security directive response, using hours of
engineering time that produce no finding.

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

The operator is a gas transmission operator in the United States, as its own requirement states, running a
gas transmission estate of more than 3,000 miles of pipe, more than a dozen compressor stations,
several gas control centers, and a compressor fleet of more than 100 units. The stations carry three
generations of remote terminal units and programmable logic controllers on mixed backhaul: leased lines,
licensed radio and intermittent cellular. Each station sits inside a hazardous area classification that
constrains what may be installed and where. The people in the loop, by role, are the pipeline controllers
who work shifts and own the detect, validate and initiate sequence for any leak alarm; the control
engineer who signs the zone and conduit design; maintenance planners who turn diagnoses into work
orders; the compliance owner who answers to the regulators; and the plan owner responsible for the
security implementation plan the whole build must fit inside. The named systems the design reads are

four systems of record: the historian, the alarm and event stream, the computerized maintenance
management system, and the corporate identity directory. The places are the stations, the line between
them, and the control centers where every decision finally lands.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 2

Four Systems Each See One Slice of the Line

The historian, the alarm and event stream, the CMMS and the security tooling each hold a
true but partial picture, and the question that matters most, whether this alarm is a leak,
needs all of them at once.

Chapter 1 set out the question. This chapter explains why no system the operation already runs can
answer it.

2.1 What Each System Sees

The historian: the CPM and fleet health models stand on the pressure, flow, vibration and temperature
tags the operator already collects; the historian is the system of record for the line.

The alarm and event stream: the assistant must explain alerts in the context of the alarms controllers
already see, and the 192.631 alarm management reviews need off-scan and inhibited-point records.

CMMS: the operator's single CMMS holds the maintenance records the fleet health models join to, and it
is where a diagnosis becomes a work order with an owner and a due date.

Corporate identity directory: every console, the registry, the observability stack and the work surface log in
through one identity realm federated to the operator's existing directory, so leavers lose access when the
directory removes them.

     Figure 2. Four systems, each seeing one part of the answer. The question needs all of them in one place at once.

2.2 What None of Them See Together

Each holds one slice, and the question needs all of them in one place at once, which today is done by
hand at the cadence of whoever has the time.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 3

The Hard Rules of the Line Shape Every Layer

No writes to field devices, passive listening only, open weights on premises and a controller
who decides every action are not features to add later but constraints that fix the architecture
before any component is chosen.

Chapter 2 showed four true but partial pictures that no manual effort can join at the speed of a control
room. This chapter states the hard rules that shape every layer of the answer before any component is
chosen, because in this industry the constraints are not features to add later.

3.1 The System Never Writes to a Field Device

The first rule comes from the operator's requirement in its own words: the system never writes to a field
device. On a gas transmission estate, shutdown and control authority lives in certified control paths that
have been qualified under the pipeline safety rules, and no analytics layer may sit inside that authority.
This is hard in this industry because the commercially tempting design, an agent that closes a valve or
trims a setpoint when its model is confident, is exactly the design the requirement forbids. The
consequence is fixed early: the control room assistant drafts responses and a controller decides every

action, and shutdown stays with the existing certified paths. Every interface to the operational technology
side is therefore read-only by design, not by policy.

3.2 The Network Is Listened To, Never Probed

The second rule is passive monitoring. The stations run three generations of remote terminal units and
programmable logic controllers on mixed serial and Internet Protocol links, and active scanning of such
equipment carries real risk of perturbing legacy devices that were never built to be queried by strangers.
So the operational technology network sensors listen on network taps and switched port analyzer ports
only, decoding protocol traffic as it passes, never probing. The hardness here is coverage: passive
protocol decoding can be blind on pure-serial segments with no Internet Protocol visibility, which is why a
per-station visibility survey with a documented serial-gateway decision is a phase one workstream rather
than an assumption.

3.3 The Weights Live on the Operator's Premises

The third rule is open weights on premises. The operator must own the models it depends on, on its own
hardware, with no data leaving its boundary and no vendor able to withdraw capability. This is hard
because the model market pushes the other way: most frontier capability is served from someone else's
cloud under someone else's license, and some capable open-weight models are published by entities on
the United States Entity List, an untenable provenance for a critical infrastructure owner. The design
therefore commits to plain permissive grants, Apache-2.0 and MIT, with no field-of-use restriction, and
treats license terms as a first-class selection criterion alongside accuracy.

3.4 A Controller Decides Every Action

The fourth rule is the human loop. Every alert the system raises competes for controller attention against
a written alarm management plan with monthly reviews under 192.631, and alarm fatigue is a
documented regulatory concern in its own right. The design answers by setting the alert budget before the
thresholds: the assistant console is advisory and adds zero alarms to the existing stream, every assistant
alert is counted in the annual plan review, and every model that could influence a decision runs in shadow
mode beside the incumbent alarms before any controller-facing alert exists. The controller's detect,
validate and initiate sequence for a leak alarm is preserved, not automated around.

3.5 Scoping Decisions and Their Costs

The constraints above force scoping decisions, and each buys something at a cost the operator accepts
knowingly. Table 1 records the three that shape the most downstream structure.

One Stack Runs From the Taps to the Consoles

A single layered stack carries every signal from passive network taps and field sensors
through adapters into one object model, and back out to the services and surfaces the
controllers and engineers actually use.

Chapter 3 fixed the constraints that shape everything downstream: open weights on the operator's own
hardware, no writes to any field device, security directive evidence that generates itself from monitoring,
and detection that keeps working when a station's backhaul drops. This chapter lays out the one stack
that satisfies all four together, by settling once, at the bottom, how every signal enters and, at the top, who
acts on it.

4.1 Bottom to Top, One Direction of Flow

The architecture is three layers with a single direction of flow. Below sit the systems of record the operator
already runs: the historian holding the pressure, flow, vibration and temperature tags, the alarm and event
stream the controllers already watch, the CMMS that owns the equipment master and the work orders,
and the corporate identity directory. In the middle sits one object model, at version 0.9, which is the only
layer that writes. Above it sit the applications and agents: ten services that do the monitoring, forecasting,
detection and explanation, and seven surfaces where named people decide. Nothing replaces a system
of record, and nothing above the model talks to anything below it except through the model.

The pattern fits a pipeline estate because such estates accrete systems over decades and cannot be
swapped for a clean slate; the design reads each record where it stands. The layer split also carries the
constraints directly. Read-only adapters honor the no-write rule at the boundary, and the single write path
through the model is what makes the security directive evidence auditable: every record in it can be
traced to the source event that produced it.

Figure 3 shows the layered stack with its counts: four sources, three adapter families, fourteen objects,

in KRaft mode as the event backbone, InfluxDB 3 Core for time series, MediaMTX for video ingest, K3s
for edge orchestration, Harbor as the air-gapped artifact and model registry, CVAT for labeling and
retraining, linuxptp with chrony for time synchronization, Keycloak for identity, and Prometheus with

Fourteen Objects Turn Station Data Into One Argument

The object model gives stations, segments, compressor units, OT devices, alarms, leak
events, work orders and security directive controls typed links, so a query can walk from a
methane reading to the controller who confirmed it and the work order that closed it.

Chapter 4 carried every signal from the taps and sensors through the adapters into one object model.
This chapter opens that model, names every object in it, and shows what the typed links let a query do
that a document store cannot.

5.1 Fourteen Objects and Their Typed Links

The model holds fourteen objects. The sites are the compressor station, carrying station number, state,
RTU and PLC generations, backhaul type and hazardous area classification reference, and the meter
station as the measurement record, carrying set pressure, meter run and remote telemetry type; the two
are kept separate because they anchor in different systems and are reconciled by link rather than by
merge. The assets are the pipeline segment, with maximum allowable operating pressure, diameter and
wall thickness, class location, inline inspection assessment date and high-consequence-area flag; the
compressor unit, with type, running hours, last overhaul date, vibration and temperature points and mean
time between failures; and the OT device, with device class, vendor and firmware version, address,

approved logic fingerprint and last-seen time. The actor is the pipeline controller, with shift, qualification
and roles in normal, abnormal and emergency conditions. The events are the alarm, the leak or abnormal
operation event and the remote access session. The records are the work order and the security directive
control. The systems are the historian and the CMMS. The document is the hazardous area classification.

The typed links join them into one argument. A station links to its hazardous area classification and hosts
its OT devices; compressor units link to the stations they run at; an alarm escalates to the leak event it
raised; a leak event links to the controller who confirmed it and to the work order that closed it; work
orders link to the CMMS record that holds them; remote access sessions link to the OT device they
reached. Figure 4 draws every object and every link, with the leak event in focus as the object the
argument turns on.

That focus is what a query can reach. Starting from a methane reading at a station, a query walks to the
station's hazardous area classification, to the CPM alarm record, to the controller who confirmed the
event, to the work order with its owner and due date, and to the regulatory report reference, in one
traversal. A document store returns whatever matches the words of a search; it cannot walk a typed link,
so the same argument has to be reassembled by hand each time. The link from a diagnosis to an owned
work order exists because pipework left unmaintained has failed through local corrosion in prosecuted
cases (HSE n.d.), and a major hydrocarbon release from exactly that neglect drew a fine in a recent
prosecution (HSE 2025).

Four Sources, Three Adapters, No Direct Access

Every source system enters through one of three adapter families that guarantee
provenance, ordering and read-only behavior, and nothing ever reads a field device directly.

Chapter 5 opened the object model and its typed links. This chapter describes how data gets into it: four
sources, three adapter families, and no direct access to anything.

6.1 The Sources and Their Provenance

Four named source systems feed the model, all read only. The historian is the system of record for the
line, holding the pressure, flow, vibration and temperature tags the CPM and fleet health models stand on;
its provenance class is the operator's own. The alarm and event stream is the set of alarms controllers
already see, plus the off-scan and inhibited-point records the alarm management reviews need; also the
operator's own. The CMMS holds the equipment master and the work order history the fleet health
models join to, and it is where a diagnosis becomes a work order with an owner and a due date; the
operator's own. The corporate identity directory is domain-typical, the identity realm an operator of this
size already runs, federated so that access ends when the directory ends it. Figure 5 maps each source,
its provenance class and its adapter path into the model.

          Figure 5. The 4 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

6.2 What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

Three adapter families carry the four sources. The Telemetry adapter takes historian tags and sensor
streams; the Ops systems adapter takes the alarm stream and the CMMS; the Integration adapter takes
the identity directory and the evidence sources behind the security directive record. The tier guarantees
five things. Every event carries a provenance stamp naming its source system, its adapter family and its
extraction time. Connections are read only, with credentials scoped to read at the adapter. Ordering is
preserved from source to backbone. No adapter ever addresses a field device: signals arrive from the
historian's open APIs, with OPC UA and MQTT where IP links exist, and from the passive taps, never by
probing the RTUs and PLCs. Each feed is translated into the object vocabulary, so services never see a
raw tag name, and backpressure is absorbed at the adapter so a slow consumer never stalls a source.

6.3 The Event Backbone

The backbone is Apache Kafka 4.3.x in KRaft mode, which needs no separate coordination service.
Ordering holds because producers key events by station and tag, so each station's events keep their
sequence within a partition even when a station resynchronizes after hours of lost backhaul. Delivery is at
least once, made safe by idempotent writes keyed to the source's own sequence number, so a replay
after a reconnect cannot double-count a reading. Buffering lives on the station edge nodes as store-and-
forward queues sized for the agreed survival window at the measured message rate, doubled, and every
display and every assistant answer marks data that arrived through the buffer as stale. Replication runs in
the control center cluster, so the loss of a node costs no evidence. Model and container artifacts enter
through the Harbor registry by a separately approved change path under management of change, never
back through the one-way path out of the OT zone.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 7

Detection Lives at the Station, Reasoning in the Center

Forecasting and camera detection run on station edge hardware sized to survive backhaul
loss, while the frontier assistant and retrieval models run in the control center, and only
telemetry and evidence cross the one-way boundary.

Chapter 6 described how every source enters through an adapter and lands on the event backbone. This
chapter decides where the four models actually run, and one physical fact settles most of it: the stations
sit on intermittent cellular backhaul, so anything that must keep working when the link drops has to run
where the data is born.

7.1 Two Tiers, Each with Its Own Arithmetic

The edge tier lives in the station cabinet. Chronos-2 forecasts the pressure, flow, vibration and
temperature tags and thresholds its residual for anomaly; at about 0.48 GB of weights at 32 bit, or about
0.24 GB at 16 bit, it leaves most of the station edge module's memory free. RF-DETR watches the
cameras for the compressor package, gas plume, person, service truck, vent event and hot spot classes;
the Apache-licensed Nano to Large checkpoints occupy about 61 to 68 MB at 16 bit, and the 2XL size
about 254 MB. Both are served by Triton Inference Server on K3s, on volume-production modules in 7W
to 60W envelopes chosen by thermal envelope rather than part number, and both keep detecting through
backhaul loss. That offline survival is why they sit at the station: deterioration of containment pipework
progresses locally and silently between maintenance rounds until the pipework fails (HSE n.d.), and
continuous local signatures are what catch it.

The central tier lives in the control centers. Mistral Large 3 675B (Instruct), the frontier model behind the
control room assistant, the compliance agent and the work surface, publishes at FP8 as about 682 GB of
weights, which fits a single node of eight 141 GB HBM-class GPUs with headroom for serving overhead;
the NVFP4 build of the same model fits a node of 80 GB HBM-class GPUs. BGE-M3 runs beside it for
retrieval at about 1.1 GB at fp16, negligible against the same node. Figure 6 sets the two tiers side by
side, with what runs on each and what crosses between them.

         Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.

7.2 The Latency Budget Is Ordered by Who Waits

Three loops carry three budgets. The station loop closes entirely on station hardware, so camera
detections and forecast residuals arrive at the speed of the local models, never at the speed of the link.
The control room loop is conversational: a controller asks the assistant to explain an alert, retrieval and
generation run on the central node, and the answer lands in the time a person reads a screen; the
console is advisory and adds zero alarms to the HMI, so every new alert is counted inside the alarm
management plan reviews required by 49 CFR 192.631(e) rather than competing outside them. The
evidence loop is batch: security directive evidence, ontology maintenance and compliance records
generate on schedule, not on demand. Stale data is marked on every display and every answer, so a
controller never mistakes a store-and-forward replay for a live reading.

7.3 One Way Out, One Approved Path In

Only telemetry, detections, forecast residuals and evidence records cross the boundary, through a
hardware-enforced one-way diode out of the OT zone with no return path to misconfigure. Model updates
never travel that conduit: they enter through a separately approved change path under management of
change, pulled from the air-gapped Harbor registry. When the link fails, station buffers sized for the
agreed survival window at the measured message rate, doubled, hold everything until the connection
returns, and every display marks what is stale. When power fails at a station, detection stops with the
station, and the gap in the record is itself visible in the observability stack. When the update path fails, the
station keeps running its last approved weights and flags the version skew, and Prometheus with Grafana
shows the divergence until the change is resynchronized. Leak-relevant detection never depends on any
of these paths, because a loss of primary containment at a single facility can escalate in minutes (DOT
2022).

8.1 Four Models, Four Jobs

Figure 7 stacks the four models over the ground they run on, from the station cabinets to the control-
center node. Mistral Large 3 675B (Instruct) is a 675B-parameter mixture-of-experts model published at
FP8, about 682 GB of weights, fitting a single node of eight 141 GB HBM-class GPUs. Its role is the
agentic work surface and ontology maintenance: it runs the control room assistant, the compliance agent
and the work surface entirely inside the control centers. Its license is Apache-2.0, a plain grant with no
field-of-use restriction and no Entity-List exposure, and that is precisely why it was chosen over GLM 5.3
open weights, whose publisher sits on the US Entity List, an untenable provenance for a United States
critical infrastructure owner.

Chronos-2 does zero-shot multivariate and covariate-informed forecasting on the pressure, flow, vibration
and temperature tags, with the residual thresholded for anomaly. It weighs about 0.48 GB at 32 bit and

about 0.24 GB at 16 bit, is Apache-2.0 licensed, and runs on the station edge boxes so detection keeps
working through backhaul loss.

RF-DETR carries station camera scene detection. Only the Apache-2.0 sizes are used: the Nano to Large
checkpoints at about 61 to 68 MB at 16 bit and the 2XL size at about 254 MB, published at BF16. It is
fine-tuned on the operator's own site footage with CVAT for the six detection classes, exports to the edge
NPU, and the exact version is pinned so the Plus sizes under PML 1.0 never enter the air-gapped
registry.

BGE-M3 provides retrieval embeddings for maintenance history and procedure search. It is MIT licensed,
carries an 8K context window, and produces hybrid dense and sparse retrieval from one pass, which
keeps tag names, error codes and part numbers findable where pure dense embeddings lose them. It
weighs about 2.27 GB at FP32, about 1.1 GB at fp16 and about 0.6 GB at 8 bit, and runs beside the work
surface in the control center.

9.1 Two Phases, One Gate and Full Coverage

Figure 8 shows the whole path. Phase 1 carries 16 items across six workstreams: the data foundation,
OT network monitoring, compressor fleet health, line leak detection, the control room assistant, and the
phase one pilot that binds them at the pilot stations. Its single exit gate is API RP 1130, the recommended
practice that governs computational pipeline monitoring: the line leak detection workstream does not
leave the phase until the sensitivity-versus-false-alarm test has been run for each segment and the per-
segment detectable limit has been written down as an acceptance test. Phase 2 carries one item, the
fourteen station fleet rollout, and inherits every phase one artifact unchanged: the fourteen object model,
the adapters, the agentic memory and the monitoring console. Requirement coverage closes at three
requirements covered, none partial and none open: passive OT monitoring with self-generating TSA
security directive evidence, compressor fleet health from vibration and performance data, and leak and
abnormal operation detection with the assistant that explains each alert and drafts the response.

9.2 What the Rollout Measures

The pilot measures four things. First, the per-segment detectable limit, from the sensitivity-versus-false-
alarm tests, so every controller knows what mass balance can and cannot see. Second, shadow
agreement: every model that could influence a decision runs beside the incumbent alarms, and what is
counted is agreement and disagreement against the record controllers already trust, not a claimed
accuracy. Third, alarm load: the assistant console is advisory and adds zero alarms to the HMI, and every
assistant alert is counted in the monthly review the alarm management plan already requires. Fourth,
work order conversion: how many model-raised diagnoses the CMMS work orders confirm, because
deferred maintenance is how contained pipework becomes a release, as the corrosion failure behind a
prosecuted hydrocarbon case shows (HSE n.d.) and as the fine that followed seven years of
unmaintained pipework confirms (HSE 2025).

9.4 Lessons

Shadow the flags before anyone trusts them. A controller-facing alert exists only after the shadow
record against the incumbent alarms justifies it, and the same rule applies to the health models and the
camera detections: nothing crosses from the machine to the console on the machine's own testimony.

Set the alarm budget before the thresholds. Every new alert competes for controller attention under a
written plan with monthly reviews, so the budget is fixed first and the thresholds are tuned into it, not the
other way round.

Sign the boundary with the control engineer, not only IT. The OT and IT zone-and-conduit sketch is a
phase one deliverable signed by the control engineer, because the person who owns the stations, not the
person who owns the firewall, knows what a mistake there costs.

9.5 What Is Still Open

The station inference server class, the camera class, the enclosures, site networking, positioning and the
frontier cluster class all stand as open class decisions, chosen by thermal envelope and duty rather than
part number; settling the camera class would fix detection latency at the fence line, and settling the
inference server class decides whether the work surface shares a node with the retrieval stack. The
backhaul survival window is an agreed number still to be fixed, and it sizes the store-and-forward buffers.
The US methane and pipeline leak rule versions changed status repeatedly between 2024 and 2026, so
rule versions are encoded as objects and repair timelines follow the operator's compliance team; settling
a rule version would let the evidence record carry firm dates instead of objects. A loss of primary
containment at a gas handling facility shows why detection quality is worth this patience (DOT 2022).

The Operator Owns the Models, Record and Boundary

Everything the design builds, from the object model and the fine-tuned weights to the
decision record and the station boundary, remains the operator's property and stays inside its
own security plan.

Chapter 9 set the phases, the gate and the measurements. This chapter settles the question the operator
asked at the start: when the rollout is finished, whose is it.

10.1 What the Operator Holds

The object model is the operator's: fourteen objects, from the station and the pipeline segment to the
security directive control, with their typed links, their status vocabularies and the hazardous area
classification document they anchor to, held in the operator's own store on its own hardware. The weights
are the operator's: Mistral Large 3 675B, Chronos-2 and the RF-DETR Apache sizes sit under Apache-
2.0, and BGE-M3 under MIT, licenses with no field-of-use restriction, so the fine-tune on the operator's
own station footage and the residual thresholds tuned on its own telemetry are property it can keep, move
or retire without a vendor's consent. The decision record is the operator's: every confirmed leak event,
every controller response, every cleared non-leak and every deferred work order is a kept object the next
decision reads, and it is never used to update model weights. The boundary is the operator's: the
hardware-enforced one-way path out of each station OT zone, the identity realm federated to the
corporate directory, and the evidence record scoped to the measures the operator's own security plan
states, with the operator retaining sole responsibility for compliance even where operation is delegated.
The system never writes to a field device, and shutdown stays with the certified control paths, so what the
operator owns is intelligence, not control.

10.2 The Offer Behind the Design

CodeNinja designed this system on CodeNinja Praxis, its platform for designing physical AI systems, and
the design maps directly onto what CodeNinja builds: the passive OT monitoring, the compressor fleet
health models, the tested computational pipeline monitoring and the methane and camera sensing at the
highest risk stations are Adaptive Operations; the control room assistant that ranks, explains and drafts a
response for a named controller to decide is Decision Systems; the fourteen object model is Hyper
Ontology; the surface on which the operator's controllers and engineers build their own agents over that
model is Hyper Pragma; the kept record of decisions and outcomes that the next decision reads is Hyper
Engram; the own hardware, the open-weight licenses and the in-country, premises-bound operation are
Sovereign Infrastructure; and the design itself, with its recorded reading and its eight lenses, was
produced on Praxis.

PA R T I V · C O N C L U S I O N

One Read-Only Model of the Line, Owned Outright
The design is a single argument assembled from an estate's own signals: passive OT taps, compressor
vibration and temperature, line pressure and flow, methane sensing and cameras at the highest risk
stations, all landing in one object model from which detection, fleet health, control room explanation and
security directive evidence are all read. Every layer of it runs on hardware the operator owns, under
licenses that let the operator hold its own weights, with a one-way boundary out of every station zone and
no write path to any field device; the assistant drafts and explains, and a controller decides.

Running the same shape elsewhere takes three things the estate already has: systems of record worth
reading, stations where passive taps and diodes can be fitted without touching control logic, and people
accountable for the alarm plan and the security directive evidence who will own the thresholds and the
record. The stack, the object model, the adapter discipline and the placement rules travel; the ontology is
re-anchored in the new operator's own stations, units, segments and rules, and the first gate stays cheap
because shadow mode comes before any controller ever sees a flag.

PA R T I V · C H A P T E R 11

How Praxis Contextualized and Reasoned This Design

Every design in the series is produced on Praxis, and this chapter records the ask, the
reading and the eight lenses so any choice in the paper can be traced back to what justified
it.

Chapter 10 established that everything the design builds stays with the operator. This final chapter
records how the design itself was reasoned, so any choice in the paper can be traced back to what
justified it (Figure 9). Every design in the Vertical-Driven Architectures series is produced on Praxis, the

design team platform for designing physical AI systems. This chapter lists what was asked, what was
read, and what each of the eight lenses contributed, and it closes on where the reasoning lands.

11.1 Contextualizing the Ask

The ask, in the operator's own words, was passive OT network monitoring at the stations and the gas
control centers with TSA security directive evidence generated from the monitoring, compressor fleet
health from vibration and performance data, leak and abnormal operation detection from pressure and
flow plus methane sensing and cameras at high risk stations, and a control room assistant that explains
alerts and drafts responses for a controller to decide, never writing to field devices, under PHMSA and
TSA rules, with open weights on premises. Praxis assigned the design to the Physical AI family and the
Oil and Gas industry, with the country placed by the operator's own requirement. The room held 1401
records; 119 were read in full during the design and the remaining 1282 are available on request.

title: Wayside Trend Watch: Predictive Maintenance From Wayside Detectors for a Freight Railroad in the United States
text:
V E R T I C A L - D R I V E N A R C H I T E C T U R E S · R A I L & T R A N S P O R TAT I O N · D E S I G N E D W I T H P R A X I S · O C T O B E R 2 0 2 6

Wayside Trend Watch: Days of Warning
Before Any Stop Alarm
For a freight railroad in the United States, the system trends every car and locomotive across
its wayside detectors into one ranked queue that mechanical and track teams act on days or
weeks before a stop alarm, with people deciding every set out and no train ever stopped or
signal changed by software.

CodeNinja Engineering Team

For the chief mechanical officer and the track and maintenance-of-way leads, and the mechanical, reliability, data and
platform engineers who would build and run it.

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-
world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for
designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

ABSTRACT

A Failure Is a Trend Before It Is an Alarm
The question a freight railroad in the United States needs answered is which serialized bearing, wheelset,
traction motor or track segment is degrading, how fast, and what a named person should do about it
before a single-reading stop alarm fires on the dispatcher's desk. It cannot be answered today because
the 29 wayside detectors judge every axle in isolation, the locomotive condition data that exists sits in
shop systems, the contractor geometry and rail flaw reports arrive as PDFs, and no query can walk from
one detector pass through the car's identity, its work order history and its interchange record to the
decision that reading should trigger. The single-reading alarm path stays as it is; what is missing is the
weeks of evidence that precede it.

The design joins 5 named source systems through 2 adapter families into one object model of 14 objects
that the railroad owns, served by 9 services and surfaced on 5 surfaces, with 4 open-weights models: D-
FINE and PP-OCRv6 run on the wayside NPU beside the four cameras of a new yard-entry portal so raw

video never leaves the site and only detections, reporting-mark OCR strings and short evidence frames
cross the link, Chronos-2 trends the per-axle detector series centrally, and gpt-oss-120b serves the one
ranked queue and the ontology-maintaining agents from a single 141 GB card in the railroad's own data
center. A pilot set of locomotives carries continuous traction motor and axle bearing sensing, the existing
detector alarm path to the dispatcher is untouched, and every set out and every slow order is decided by
a person whose name is on the record.

The paper covers the problem and the join failure, the four constraints, the layered stack, the fourteen
objects and their typed links, ingestion through adapters, where each model runs and why, the models
and their licenses, the three phases with their seventeen items and gates, what the rollout measures, who
owns what the design builds, and closes with the chapter showing how Praxis contextualized and
reasoned the design.

Figure 1. Wayside Trend Watch on one page: the sources the operation already runs, one object model, what it computes,
                                             and the person who decides.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

A Bearing Degrades for Weeks Before the Alarm Sounds

A hot bearing, a wearing wheel and a settling track all announce themselves in readings the
railroad already collects, but each reading is judged alone and the trend that precedes the
alarm is never assembled.

The abstract promised a single ranked queue built from detectors the railroad already runs. Before any
design can earn that promise, the problem has to be stated exactly: the question the operation needs
answered, what it costs the industry when that question goes unanswered, and the shape of the
operation that must live with the answer.

1.1 The Question the Operation Needs Answered

The mechanical and track teams need one question answered continuously: which serialized bearing,
wheelset, traction motor or track segment is degrading, how fast, and what should be done about it by
when, days or weeks before any single reading trips a stop alarm. Answering it requires data the
operation already holds in fragments: per-axle readings from every pass of every car across the wayside
detector network, with ambient temperature and train speed as covariates; work orders and car and
locomotive master data, so a trend can be read against what was repaired and when; and interchange
records, so a flagged foreign car can reach the right owner. The answer must satisfy federal railroad
safety rules covering track, freight car, locomotive and brake inspection under 49 CFR Parts 213, 215,
229 and 232, the Federal Railroad Administration's guidance that railroads evaluate their policies for hot
bearing wayside detectors (Federalregister 2023), industry guidance on axle bearing condition monitoring
by trackside and onboard means (RSSB n.d.), and the interchange rules of the industry's equipment
registry.

1.2 The Documented Cost of the Problem

The cost of a bearing or wheel run to failure is documented in the public record. In March 2023 the
Federal Railroad Administration issued Safety Advisory 2023-01, directing railroads to evaluate their
policies and procedures for the use and maintenance of hot bearing wayside detectors after a derailment
in which a bearing degraded across detector passes without a stop-level reading (Federalregister 2023).
A peer reviewed study in the Transportation Research Record found that in-service failures of railroad
rolling stock cause train delay and economic impact, and that railcar condition feeds directly into that cost
(DOI 2011). A structural wagon failure at speed, investigated and publicly reported, shows the same
shape in a different component: degradation visible in hindsight, invisible in operation (NSW 2012). Each
failure mode shares one property, that the evidence existed in readings before the event and was never
assembled into a trend anyone acted on.

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

The operator is a freight railroad in the United States, operating across multiple subdivisions with a mixed
fleet of cars and locomotives. Its wayside estate counts 29 existing detectors: 22 hot box and hot wheel
detectors, 4 wheel impact load detectors, 2 acoustic bearing detectors and 1 automated wheel profile
system at the busiest yard entry. The design adds a four-camera portal at that yard entry, covering the left
side, right side, wheel line and a throat overview, plus pilot vibration and temperature sensing on
locomotive traction motors and axle bearings. The people in the loop, by role, are the mechanical
supervisors who own the queue, the car inspectors and shop craft who confirm and repair, the track
supervisors who own geometry and rail flaws, the dispatchers who keep the single stop decision, and a
small information technology team of five who run whatever is built. The physical environments are
wayside detector bungalows, an exposed yard throat, locomotive and car shops, running subdivisions
and one central data center. The regulatory ground is federal railroad safety rules and industry
interchange rules. The design counts five named source systems, two adapter families, fourteen objects,

nine services, five surfaces and four models, handed over in three gated phases against four
requirements.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 2

Every System Sees One Slice of the Car

The detector network, the maintenance system, the interchange records, the dispatch
channel and the contractor reports each hold a slice of the truth, and no query can walk from
any one of them to the answer.

Chapter 1 set out the question. This chapter explains why no system the operation already runs can
answer it.

2.1 What Each System Sees

Wayside detector network the 29 existing detectors are the primary sensing this design trends; every
pass of every car must be ingested with per-axle resolution

Railroad maintenance system (CMMS/EAM) work orders and car and locomotive master data are the
joins that turn a reading into a decision and a repair

Railinc Umler and interchange services a flagged foreign car must reach the right owner, and the
engineer's intake answer is direct Railinc/Umler integration

Dispatcher advisory channel the system advises and never acts: trend advisories and portal findings must
reach the dispatcher through a path that touches no signal, train control or PTC system

Contractor geometry and rail flaw reports the engineer's intake answer digitises the contractor PDFs into
the same trending pipeline and single queue from day one, so track degradation joins the rolling stock
picture

     Figure 2. Five systems, each seeing one part of the answer; the question needs all of them in one place at once.

2.2 What None of Them See Together

Each holds one slice, and the question needs all of them in one place at once, which today is done by
hand at the cadence of whoever has the time.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 3

Four Constraints Shape Everything Downstream

Advisory-only operation, open weights in the railroad's own environment, no reduction of any
regulated inspection, and a small mechanical desk set the boundaries every later choice in
this design must respect.

Chapter 2 showed that the answer lives across five systems no query can span. This chapter sets the
four constraints that bound every later choice in the design, then records what those bounds bought and
what they cost.

3.1 The System Advises and Never Acts

The first constraint is advisory-only operation: the design must never stop a train or change a signal. This
is hard in rail because the industry already has an automated stop path, the single-reading alarm to the
dispatcher, and hardening a second one would demand a safety case nobody wants to write for a trend
system. So the design connects to no vital circuit, no train control path and no positive train control

system; advisories ride a channel beside the alarm, never in front of it, and dispatch keeps the stop
decision entirely.

3.2 Open Weights in the Railroad's Own Environment

The second constraint is sovereign: every model must run as open weights on the railroad's own
hardware, in its own data center, with no data leaving its boundary. This is hard in the United States at the
needed scale, because the US-origin open-weights shelf is thin and one major frontier vendor sits on the
US Entity List, which removes it from consideration for a critical-infrastructure buyer. The arithmetic
settles the sizing: the work surface model at 117 billion parameters ships as a checkpoint of about 65.2
GB, its MoE weights in MXFP4 and the rest at 16 bit; with a 1.2 planning factor for KV cache and
activations the card must hold about 78.2 GB, and one 141 GB high-bandwidth-memory card holds it with
about 63 GB to spare.

3.3 No Regulated Inspection Is Reduced

The third constraint is that the design claims no waiver and reduces no visual or periodic inspection under
49 CFR Parts 213, 215, 229 or 232. This is hard because sensing anywhere near inspection practice
reads as automation of union work, and the automated inspection waiver fights began exactly there. The
design's answer is behavioral: the first phases change no inspection frequency and no job duty, crafts see
the same dashboards as management, and the consultation record is written as a project deliverable as it
happens.

3.4 A Small Mechanical Desk Sets the Alert Budget

The fourth constraint is human: the mechanical desk is small, and alert volume above what it can act on
turns the queue into noise. The design therefore fixes an alert budget with the supervisors before any
threshold is set, keeps the ranked queue below that budget line, and reports acknowledge, ignore and
action rates weekly. Every set out is decided by a person.

3.5 Scoping Decisions

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 4

One Stack Runs From the Detectors to the Queue

Two adapter families feed one object model, nine services and five surfaces, with nothing
replacing the systems of record and no data leaving the railroad's environment.

Chapter 3 fixed the four constraints that shape everything downstream: the systems of record stay in
place, the data stays inside the railroad's environment, the single-reading stop alarm to the dispatcher
stays exactly as it is, and every set out stays with a person. This chapter lays out the stack that satisfies
those constraints, layer by layer, from the detector bungalows to the ranked queue.

4.1 The Pattern and Why It Fits

The pattern is a deliberate sandwich: systems of record below, one object model in the middle,
applications and agents above. Below sit the five sources the design reads and never replaces: the
wayside detector network, the maintenance system, the Railinc Umler and interchange services, the
dispatcher advisory channel, and the contractor geometry and rail flaw reports. In the middle, the object
model v0.9 holds the fourteen objects that turn per-axle readings into one argument, with the telemetry
store chosen by class beside it for the raw series. Above, nine services and five surfaces do the work,
and an agentic work surface maintains the ontology itself.

This shape fits a railroad for three reasons. First, no railroad can swap its maintenance system or its
detector network for a platform, and the advisory posture the Federal Railroad Administration expects
around hot bearing detector policies presupposes that the detector network and its alarm path remain

Fourteen Objects Turn Detector Noise Into One
Argument

Fourteen objects and their typed links let a query walk from a flagged reading to the
serialized bearing, its wheelset, its car, the work order that fixed it last time and the track
segment it crossed, which no document store can do.

Chapter 4 laid the stack from the detectors to the queue, and its middle layer was named but not opened.
This chapter opens it: the fourteen objects, the typed links between them, and the one recorded object
where a trend becomes a person's decision.

5.1 Every Object and Its Typed Links

The model holds fourteen objects in four kinds. Seven are assets: Freight Car, Locomotive, Axle Bearing
(Roller Bearing), Wheelset, Traction Motor, Wayside Detector and Track Segment. One is a measure:
Detector Reading. Five are records: Trend Flag, Work Order, Track Geometry Exception, Rail Flaw
Indication and AAR Interchange Record. One is an event: Train. Figure 4 shows every object and every
typed link between them, with the trend flag as the focal object.

The links are what make the argument. A wheelset is paired with the axle bearing that shares its axle
position; a traction motor is mounted on a locomotive; a wayside detector produced each detector
reading; a reading was taken by a train and measures a specific serialized bearing and wheelset; a track
segment carries geometry exceptions and sets the detector spacing against which a warning interval is
judged. Because axle bearings and wheelsets are keyed to serialized components rather than to cars, a
bearing keeps its baseline and its wear history across wheel changes, car renumbers and interchanges,
which is exactly the continuity that condition monitoring standards for axle bearings assume (RSSB n.d.).

A query can therefore walk a path no document store can: from a flagged reading, to the bearing it
measured, to the wheelset beside it, to the car that carries both, to the work order that fixed that bearing
last time, to the track segment where the reading was taken, to the open geometry exception on that
same segment. A document store can hold each of those facts; it cannot traverse them, because the joins
are not documents but typed links the query engine follows.

5.2 The Human Loop and the Hosting Posture

The human loop lives in the trend flag, which carries a disposition and a disposer: every flag stays Open
until a named person confirms it, dismisses it or lets it raise a work order, and no flag ever becomes a set
out without that person. The same rule governs the track half of the queue, where a slow order remains a
person's decision.

The hosting posture keeps everything inside the railroad's boundary. The ontology runs on the operator's
own hardware in its own data center; identity and access run on Keycloak against the railroad's own
people; the only external link is the read-only Railinc Umler and interchange feed, which crosses out and
back under the railroad's own agreements. The only write path into the object model is the adapter tier
described in Chapter 6, plus the human disposition recorded through the queue surface; no source
system, no service and no agent writes any other way, and no data leaves the environment.

6.1 Five Named Sources, All Read Only

Figure 5 maps the integration. The wayside detector network is the primary sensing: all 29 detectors,
being 22 hot box and hot wheel detectors, 4 wheel impact load detectors, 2 acoustic bearing detectors
and 1 automated wheel profile system, enter with per-axle resolution so a reading resolves to one
serialized bearing. The maintenance system (CMMS/EAM) supplies work orders and car and locomotive
master data, the joins that turn a reading into a repair. Railinc Umler and interchange services give car
ownership and interchange records, so a flagged foreign car reaches the right owner. The dispatcher
advisory channel carries trend advisories and portal findings to dispatch through a path that touches no

signal, train control or PTC system. Contractor geometry and rail flaw reports arrive as PDFs that the
platform digitizes into the same trending pipeline and the same queue from day one.

All five are operator-held systems of record in the read direction, and every one carries a provenance
stamp into the object model, so any figure on any surface can be traced to the system that produced it.

       Figure 5. The 5 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

6.2 What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

The adapter tier guarantees six things. It is read only: no source system is ever written to, and no source
ever writes directly into the object model. It resolves identity: a car is identified per pass by its AEI tag
and, at the portal, by PP-OCRv6 reading the reporting mark, so the join key is settled at the edge rather
than after a video upload. It normalizes: every reading carries ambient temperature, train speed and the
detector's calibrated bias, because detector maintenance and calibration policies are precisely what the
Federal Railroad Administration asked railroads to evaluate after bearing failures (Federalregister 2023),
and a per-detector bias term is how one detector's reading is made comparable to another's. It is
idempotent: a replayed export produces one reading, keyed on detector, train, car, axle position and
timestamp. It applies back-pressure: a slow downstream service slows the adapter, never the source. And
it buffers: at the portal, inference runs on the wayside box and only detections, OCR strings and short
evidence frames cross the link, never raw video, because a cellular backhaul that drops for hours cannot
carry pixels.

6.3 The Event Backbone

The backbone is Apache Kafka 4.3.x in KRaft mode with three dedicated controllers, running in the
railroad's data center with replication across brokers. Ordering is preserved by key: every reading is
keyed on detector and axle position, so the pass sequence for one bearing arrives in the order it was
measured, which is the sequence the trending engine differentiates. Delivery is at-least-once, made safe
by the adapter's idempotent upserts, so a re-handed over message cannot double-count a reading.

Buffering happens at both ends: the wayside edge units under K3s hold store-and-forward queues that
survive backhaul outages and resynchronize when the link returns, and the portal keeps its evidence
frames local until the link can carry them. Model and artifact updates travel the other way through Harbor
as an air-gapped registry, so nothing updates from the public internet. Prometheus, Grafana and Loki
watch the whole path, and lag on any partition is the first signal that a detector, a link or an adapter needs
attention.

Chapter 6 described how every source enters through one of the two adapter families, so no detector

chapter places the four models on the hardware where they run and works the arithmetic that decides
what each tier can hold.

7.1 Two Places, No Middle Tier

Inference runs in exactly two places: the portal's wayside edge box and the railroad's central data center.
A yard-site server tier between them was weighed and set aside, because an intermediate tier adds a
failure domain a five-person IT team would have to own and nothing in the requirement needs it.

At the portal, D-FINE detects open doors, brake gear, wheel components and dragging equipment, and
PP-OCRv6 reads reporting marks, both on the octa-core NPU edge box beside the cameras. D-FINE is
about 8 MB at 16 bit in its small size and about 124 MB in its large one; PP-OCRv6's small tier is 7.7
million parameters, a few MB to about 70 MB at 16 bit, with ONNX exports that run on CPU well inside 1
GB of RAM. Together they occupy a fraction of the box, leaving the rest for the video pipeline and the
store-and-forward buffer, and car identity is resolved per pass by AEI tag and portal OCR rather than
visual tracking across frames, which is why the OCR string must become a join key at the edge rather
than after a video upload.

In the data center, Chronos-2 trends the per-axle series at about 0.48 GB as published at 32 bit, about
0.24 GB at 16 bit, small enough to sit on the trending service beside the time series store. The work
surface model sizes the tier: gpt-oss-120b, filed at 117 billion parameters, ships as a checkpoint of about
65.2 GB with its MoE weights in MXFP4 and the rest at 16 bit; the 1.2 planning factor reserves about 13

GB for KV cache and activations, so the card must hold about 78.2 GB, and one card of the 141 GB class
holds it with about 63 GB to spare. That single card, one node of one GPU, is the whole central model
tier, inside the existing data center's power and cooling. Figure 6 sets the tiers side by side with what
crosses between them.

        Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.

7.2 The Latency Budget

The budget has three horizons, each set by the physical process it serves. The portal's horizon is one
pass: detection and OCR must finish before the car clears the camera line at yard speed, and D-FINE's
card reports 2.12 to 12.89 ms at batch size 1 on a T4 for its two sizes, a figure the NPU box need not
match to stay well inside a window measured in the time a car takes to traverse the portal. The trending
horizon is one pass spacing: the forecast and residual for an axle must be ready before that axle reaches
the next detector, because the trend flag's warning interval is measured against detector spacing, and a
forecast that arrives after the next pass is not a forecast. The work surface's horizon is one supervisor
interaction: the model is a mixture of experts with roughly 5 billion active parameters, so a ranked-queue
answer completes within a working session. No requirement exceeds what its tier can meet.

7.3 What Crosses the Boundary, and What Fails

Only findings cross the cellular link: detections, OCR strings and short evidence frames, never pixels or
continuous video, because a link that drops for hours cannot carry a stream and was never asked to. The
edge box keeps detecting through an outage and buffers its outputs store-and-forward; when the link
returns, the buffered findings resynchronize into the event backbone in order and the ontology fills the
gap. The stop alarm path is untouched throughout, since it runs from detector to dispatcher on the
railroad's own wiring and this design sits beside it, never in front of it, the posture the Federal Railroad

Administration's advisory on hot bearing detectors asks railroads to evaluate for themselves
(Federalregister 2023).

Power failure at the bungalow is handled by the enclosure class: surge-protected power, a sealed case
with thermal budget for direct sun, and Network UPS Tools monitoring clean shutdown, so the box rides
through an outage and reboots into K3s orchestration with its buffer intact. Update failure is handled by
the air-gapped Harbor registry: models ship as versioned open-weight artifacts pulled inside the
boundary, and if the pull path fails the edge keeps serving the last pulled weights. Every failure leaves the
system advising more slowly, never acting differently, because there is no actuation to fail toward.

8.1 Four Models, One License Family

Figure 7 stacks the four models over the hardware they run on. Every one is Apache-2.0 open weights,
and every one runs as shipped: under the system of context nothing is trained, fine tuned or distilled for
the operator, agents improve through agentic memory rather than training runs, and detector accuracy is
governed by an evaluation harness.

gpt-oss-120b is a 120 billion parameter mixture of experts with roughly 5 billion active parameters, served
centrally on one card of the 141 GB class. Its checkpoint is 60.8 GiB, 65.2 GB of root safetensors, with
the MoE weights in MXFP4 at 4.25 bits and the rest at 16 bit, about 234 GB if expanded to full 16 bit, and
a KV cache the card files at about 4.8 GB. It serves the one queue and the ontology-maintaining agents,
and it was chosen over GLM 5.3, a 753 billion parameter model, because Zhipu AI sits on the US Entity
List and this is a United States critical-infrastructure buyer; the US-origin open-weights shelf at frontier
scale is thin, and this is the largest permissive model on it.

D-FINE is the portal's defect detector, from the real-time detection family. Apache-2.0 covers its code and
released weights with no field-of-use restriction, and the design uses the COCO checkpoints rather than
the Objects365 ones, whose terms are not commercially cleared. The card reports 42.8 to 55.8 COCO AP
across its sizes, and the small size runs on the portal's octa-core NPU box at yard speed.

PP-OCRv6 is the portal's reader, from the OCR and document parsing family: Apache-2.0 with no
revenue condition, its small tier at 7.7 million parameters with the CTC head pinned, so a car number
becomes a join key at the edge rather than after a video upload.

Chronos-2 is the trend forecaster, from the time series forecasting family, Apache-2.0. It performs zero-
shot multivariate forecasting over per-axle detector reading series with covariates, ambient temperature
and train speed, and the residual against the forecast is thresholded to raise the trend alarm. Zero-shot
matters because nothing is fine tuned for this operator. The trend alarm is the precursor reading the
single-reading stop alarm cannot see, the gap the Federal Railroad Administration's advisory on hot
bearing detectors asks railroads to evaluate (Federalregister 2023), and axle bearing monitoring by
trackside and onboard systems is an established practice with published requirements and guidance
(RSSB n.d.).

9.2 What the Rollout Measures

Shadow mode exists to measure one number before trust: lead time. For every reading that later trips the
existing stop alarm, the record shows whether a trend flag was already open on that axle or wheelset,
and how many detector passes of warning it gave, which is the warning interval the design exists to
lengthen. The queue is measured by its behavior: acknowledge, ignore and action rates reported weekly
from the start, held against the alert budget the supervisors agree before thresholds are set. The portal is
measured per detection class, all eight of them from freight car to dragging equipment, with an accuracy
record kept from day one and evidence frames captured at the worst hour of light. Each detector site is
measured for bias, mean and spread learned from live passes, so a reading is corrected against its own
detector before it joins a trend.

9.4 Lessons

Shadow the queue before anyone is asked to act on it. The existing single-reading alarm already
protects the railroad, and the federal safety advisory asked railroads to evaluate exactly how they use and
maintain hot bearing detectors (Federalregister 2023). What the new layer adds is lead time, and lead
time can only be demonstrated beside the alarm it complements; in shadow, the trend engine earns or
fails its case without a single set out depending on it.

Agree the alert budget before setting the thresholds. Thresholds set by sensitivity alone produce
more flags than a small mechanical desk can work through, and in-service failures already cost the
industry delay and money (DOI 2011), so a queue that becomes noise protects nothing. The budget
comes first, the thresholds second, and the weekly rates keep the bargain visible.

Change no inspection practice in the first phases. The disputes over automated inspection waivers
began exactly where sensing touched craft practice, and this design claims no waiver and reduces no
inspection. The crafts see the same picture management sees, and the consultation record is written
while the work happens, not after.

9.5 What Is Still Open

Three questions remain open. Whether per-axle detector history exists in exportable form: settling it
would let baselines draw on years of record instead of live passes, which would open trend flags with
more confidence and earlier. Whether the railroad's interchange data agreement covers direct registry
reads and alert filing by a new system: settling it would turn foreign-car alerts from a manual interchange
process into direct filing, and until then the existing process carries them. Whether portal accuracy holds
at night, in snow and against low sun at this yard: settling it would set the human confirmation load and
decide how high portal findings can rank in the one queue.

10.1 The Railroad Owns the Model, the Weights, the Record and the Boundary

every alert filed and every inspection request raised is kept in the agentic memory the next decision

without a training run.

The Evidence for the Next Failure Is Already Being
Recorded
In one view, the design is a join: 29 existing detectors, a camera portal and a locomotive pilot, resolved to
serialized bearings, axles and wheelsets in an object model the railroad owns, trended centrally by an
open-weights forecaster, and handed over to one ranked queue where a person decides every set out, all

of it running on the railroad's own hardware inside its own boundary while the existing stop alarm to the
dispatcher continues exactly as before.

Running the same shape elsewhere takes four things: an identity key that ties each reading to a
serialized component rather than to a vehicle, per-pass resolution fine enough to trend, an advisory-only
boundary drawn so the system never sits in front of a safety decision it does not own, and open weights
on hardware the operator controls. Wherever an operation already measures its assets on a repeated
basis, the trend that precedes the failure is in that record, and this is the shape that assembles it.

PA R T I V · C H A P T E R 11

How Praxis Contextualized and Reasoned This Design

Every choice in this design traces to recorded reading through eight lenses, and this chapter
shows the ask, what was in the room, the patterns adopted and set aside, and where the
reasoning lands.

Chapter 10 closed the ownership question: the object model, the weights, the decision record and the
boundary all stay with the railroad. Every design in this series is produced on Praxis, and this chapter is
the trace that lets a reader take any choice in the earlier chapters back to what justified it; Figure 9 shows
the whole path on one page, from the ask through the lenses to the equipment classes.

11.1 Contextualizing the Ask

The ask arrived as one paragraph from a freight railroad in the United States, with the country fixed by the
operator's own requirement: trend every car and locomotive across the wayside detectors for hot box,
wheel impact, acoustic bearing and wheel profile readings, add continuous sensing on locomotive traction
motors and a yard entry camera portal, join the result to work orders and interchange records, and give
the mechanical and track teams one queue to act days or weeks before a stop alarm, with people
deciding every set out, under FRA rules and open weights in the railroad's own environment. Praxis
assigned the design to the physical AI family in the rail and transportation vertical. What was in the room,
read in full and available on request: the European Commission's railway safety statistics (Europa 2024);
a published official investigation into the structural failure of a freight wagon (NSW 2012); the Federal
Railroad Administration safety advisory on the use and maintenance of hot bearing wayside detectors
(Federalregister 2023); the UK standards body's requirements and guidance for axle bearing condition
monitoring (RSSB n.d.); and a peer reviewed study of the delay and economic impact of in-service rolling
stock failures (DOI 2011).

AEI tag and portal OCR. And an advisory channel that runs beside the alarm rather than in front of it. Set
aside with reasons: visual tracking and trajectory forecasting, since identity is resolved per pass rather

title: Depot Operating Object Model: Ontologies for Unifying Factory Systems at a United States Vehicle Rebuild Depot
text:
V E R T I C A L - D R I V E N A R C H I T E C T U R E S · D I S C R E T E M A N U FA C T U R I N G & A U TO M O T I V E · D E S I G N E D W I T H P R A X I S
· OCTOBER 2026

Depot Operating Object Model:
Ontologies for Unifying Factory Systems
From Test Cell to Part Lot
For a discrete manufacturing and automotive operator in the United States, one operating
object model links every power pack, machine tool, test run, work order and part lot to its
system of record, keeps every machine interface read only, and leaves each release to a
named person's sign-off.

Muhammad Umar, Cofounder, CodeNinja

For the depot operations director, the maintenance and test cell leads, and the platform, controls and data engineers
who would build and run it.

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-
world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for
designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

ABSTRACT

A Failed Test Run Should Explain Itself the Same Day
When a power pack fails its scripted test run, a United States government vehicle rebuild depot needs to
know which machine cut the parts, from which lot, on which shift, and whether that machine's condition
was already drifting; that is exactly the question ontologies for unifying factory systems exist to answer,
and today the depot cannot ask it. The answer is scattered across four systems of record that never
shared a key, built from technologies that were never designed to interoperate with each other (NIST
2012). The cost of that gap is not hypothetical: a single update to a parts-ordering system halted a major
automaker's production at an estimated 350 million US dollars in lost output (ABI Research 2023), and
the depot's own version of the same failure is the failed power pack that returns for rework with no trace
of why.

The design builds one living operating object model of fourteen typed objects as a projection over five
source systems, all of which enter through a single integration adapter family over the site's OPC UA
standard, with legacy machine tools and test equipment brought on read only. Eight services run on the
model and reach people through three surfaces: two planner surfaces for schedules and condition-based
maintenance work, and one test cell surface holding each scripted run. Three Apache-2.0 models carry
the work, with condition forecasting on fanless edge boxes beside each machine group and the 117-
billion-parameter work surface model on a two-card 48 GB inference server in the depot's own server
room, so that every byte of data and every weight stays on government hardware inside the government
facility's security rules.

The paper covers the problem and the join failure, the four constraints, the layered stack, the fourteen
objects with their typed links, the ingestion path, the inference placement with its memory arithmetic, and
the three models with their licenses; readers weighing industrial ontology examples will find the object
model chapter shows every object in its recorded form. It then sets out the two-phase rollout with its item
counts and the entity resolution gate, the ownership of what the design builds, and closes with the
chapter on how Praxis contextualized and reasoned this design.

 Figure 1. Depot Operating Object Model on one page: the sources the operation already runs, one object model, what it
                                       computes, and the person who decides.
