PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

Ontologies for Unifying Factory Systems Start at the
Test Cell

A power pack that fails its test run is logged in one system while the machine that cut its
parts, the lot those parts came from and the schedule it displaces live in three others, so the
question the depot most needs to ask has never been askable.

Ontologies for unifying factory systems are usually argued as an enterprise data program whose payback
sits somewhere off in a roadmap. At a vehicle rebuild depot run by a discrete manufacturing and
automotive operator in the United States, they stand or fall on one question asked at a test cell door: this

power pack just failed its run, and no one can say which machine cut its parts, from which lots, in what
condition, or what the rework does to next week's schedule. The abstract promised a design that makes
that question askable; this chapter states the question exactly, prices the cost of leaving it unanswered,
and describes the operation that has to live with it.

1.1 The Question the Depot Needs Answered

The question, in the operator's own shape: when a power pack fails a scripted test cycle, trace the failure
back through the rebuild work order and its routing to the part lots drawn for each operation, then to the
machine and operation each lot was issued to, and to that machine's condition while the cuts were made,
then forward again to the rework the failure forces and the schedule it displaces. Answering it requires
data no single system holds: work orders and routings from production control, part lots and issue dates
from inventory, the machine asset register and maintenance history, transducer traces and limit sets from
the test cell's own software, and live machine and cell state over the site's industrial interoperability
standard. The regulatory regimes sit on top of the data. The depot is a US government site, so drawings,
programs and test data are treated as controlled unclassified information (CUI) at most, which brings the
platform enclave under NIST SP 800-171 Rev 3 and a named federal cybersecurity certification status
before any such data is processed; models must be US-origin open weights with no third-party model
service; and every machine and test cell interface is a read-only subscription, with findings published
back over the same site standard rather than written into any control.

1.2 The Documented Cost of the Problem

The cost of systems that touch but do not join is public and large. In 2023 a single update to a parts-
ordering system halted Toyota's production, and ABI Research put the lost production at about 350 million
US dollars (Automotive Manufacturing Solutions 2023; ABI Research 2023). That failure mode is not
exotic: manufacturing integration routinely combines technologies that were never designed to
interoperate with each other, which is why a change in one system surfaces as a defect in another (NIST
2012). At a rebuild depot the everyday version is quieter and compounds: an untraceable reject cannot be
closed with evidence, so it is reworked on judgment; a machine drifting out of condition cuts parts that fail
test weeks later; and each failed run consumes test cell time the schedule had already promised
elsewhere.

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

The operator runs a vehicle rebuild depot: power packs and hulls arrive, are disassembled, rebuilt across
several shops of mixed legacy machine tools that cannot be replaced, and must pass a scripted test cycle
in the power pack test cell before release. The cell carries the site's transducer suite and data bus
capture, and the design adds three observation cameras: the test cell, its control panel, and a machine
shop aisle. The people in the loop are named by role: the test cell operator who signs off every release or
return, the production planner who accepts, modifies or declines schedule proposals, the maintenance
planner who approves condition-based work orders, and the site authorizing official and information

systems security manager who own the security approvals package. The physical environments are
machining halls with mist and coolant, the test cell, the machine cabinets holding edge hardware, and the
depot's own server room, whose existing power and air cooling take two cards of the 48 GB PCIe
inference class. The regulatory ground is a government facility with the CUI enclave described above,
US-origin weight rules, and an export control regime a domestic camera install on the depot's own
premises does not trigger. The design reads five named source systems plus the one site interoperability
standard, through a single adapter family, with the test cell as the first live case and the machine shops
following in a second phase.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 2

Four Systems of Record Never Shared a Key

The production control, inventory, maintenance and test cell systems each hold a true and
complete slice of the rebuild, and none of them can see the power pack whole, which is why
four more interfaces would reproduce the problem instead of solving it.

Chapter 1 set out the question. This chapter explains why no system the operation already runs can
answer it.

2.1 What Each System Sees

Production control system owns the rebuild and rework work orders and the schedule the design must
read and inform; the object model's work order and routing objects are anchored here.

Inventory system owns the part lots the reject trace must reach: 'the parts drawn for the rework live in
inventory'.

Maintenance system owns the machine asset register and work order history, and is the destination of the
requirement's own loop: 'work raised in the maintenance system for a planner to approve'.

Test cell software where a failed test run is logged today: 'A power pack that fails its test run is logged in
the test cell's own software'; the test run and run report objects are anchored here.

OPC UA site standard the named interoperability path both ways: machine and test cell state is
subscribed read-only, and 'the result publishes to the depot's systems over the industrial interoperability
standard the site uses'.

     Figure 2. Five systems, each seeing one part of the answer. The question needs all of them in one place at once.

2.2 What None of Them See Together

Each holds one slice, and the question needs all of them in one place at once, which today is done by
hand at the cadence of whoever has the time.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 3

Sovereignty and Sign-Off Shape Every Choice
Downstream

Read-only machine interfaces, legacy equipment that cannot be replaced, a person deciding
every release and schedule change, and US-origin open weights on government hardware
together fix the shape of every layer above them.

Chapter 2 showed that each system of record sees one slice and that the shared standard carries state
without meaning. This chapter fixes the constraints that follow, because read-only interfaces,
irreplaceable legacy equipment, a person deciding every change, and US-origin weights on government
hardware together settle the shape of every layer above them before a single component is chosen.

3.1 One Object Model Over Systems That Never Shared a Key

The first goal is one operating object model linking power pack, hull, machine tool, test cell, work order,
part lot and operator role, each object anchored in its system of record. It is hard in this industry because

the four systems key the same physical world with unrelated identifiers: a power pack serial, a machine
asset tag, a lot number and a run ID were never designed to meet. Most industrial ontology examples
stop at the join; here the join must also stay live, because the model is a projection over the systems of
record rather than a new system that would add a fifth key. Where no shared key exists, a supervised
crosswalk is built and owned in the ontology with lineage, and proving the joins on live records is the first
phase gate, not an assumption.

3.2 Read-Only Sensing Beside Equipment That Cannot Be Replaced

The second goal is to bring legacy machine tools and test equipment onto the network read only, with
sensing and gateways placed beside equipment that stays. It is hard because a mixed legacy fleet has no
uniform controller: retrofit taps on stack lights and serial printer ports, IEPE accelerometers stud-mounted
per ISO 5348 on the critical tier, and current clamps must each be additive and reversible, and no write to
the site or any machine is part of the design in any phase. Safety functions are excluded outright:
interlocks, light curtains and emergency stops belong to the depot's certified systems, and the platform
observes machine state without configuring any protective device.

3.3 A Person Decides Every Release, Work Order and Schedule Change

The third goal is that the platform proposes and a person commits: the test cell operator signs off every
release or return, maintenance work is raised for a planner to approve, and schedule changes are
proposals a planner accepts, modifies or declines. It is hard because the scheduling and maintenance
software market defaults to automated optimization, and because a proposal must be good enough to
trust without ever being obeyed; a deterministic layer records every proposal and every decision so the
reasoning is auditable after the fact.

3.4 Sovereign Compute, US-Origin Weights and a Scoped CUI Enclave

The fourth goal is that data and models stay in the government's own environment, on the depot's own
hardware, with US-origin open weights and no third-party model service. It is hard because the US-origin
rule bars whole families of open weights whose publishers sit on the US Entity List, and because a
government enclave must be scoped before it is assessed: the design assumes controlled unclassified
information at most, keeps the NIST SP 800-171 enclave small with the authorizing official and
information systems security manager as named owners, and touches nothing classified. Everything from
the edge boxes to the work surface runs on site, and the server room's existing power and air cooling
take the two 48 GB inference cards without a room upgrade.

3.5 Scoping Decisions

Three decisions bound the design, each buying something specific at a stated cost, set out in Table 1: the
ontology as projection rather than replacement, the test cell as the only first live case, and baselines
rather than trained weights.

  Table 1 · Scoping Decisions

   as the first live case        schedule, proven on one cell before         the test cell proof; estate instrumentation is a

3.6 What the Design Chose Against

Each rejection below was made against a live alternative with a reason the requirement itself supplies, set
out in Table 2, closing with the boundary of what the design will not touch at all.

                     class on depot hardware                   data in the government's own environment

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 4

One Stack Reaches From Record Systems to Surfaces

Sources feed adapters, adapters feed one object model, the model feeds services, and
services feed the surfaces where planners and operators act, with the count at every layer
fixed by the layers beneath it.

Chapter 3 fixed the constraints and priced every scoping decision against them: read-only machine
interfaces, the depot's own government hardware, US-origin open weights, and a person committing
every change. This chapter lays the stack that satisfies them, and it is the working answer to ontologies
for unifying factory systems: five source systems, one adapter family, one object model of fourteen
objects, three models, eight services and three surfaces, with the count at every layer fixed by the layers
beneath it.

4.1 The Pattern and Why It Fits

The pattern is three strata. Below sit the systems of record: production control, inventory, maintenance
and the test cell software, each still owning its own keys and its own truth. In the middle sits one object
model, built as a projection over those systems rather than a migration of them, so no system of record is
replaced and none is asked to adopt another's identifier. Above sit the applications and agents: eight
deterministic services and three surfaces, with the agents running on the work surface model under the
site's own identity. The National Institute of Standards and Technology observes that manufacturing
integration routinely means combining technologies that were never designed to interoperate with each
other (NIST 2012), and a government depot that has accreted systems across decades is that
observation at full scale. Point-to-point interfaces between each pair of systems would reproduce the
vocabulary problem the design exists to solve; one projection resolves it once, for every consumer at
once. Figure 3 shows the layered stack with the count at every layer: five sources, one adapter family,
fourteen objects, three models, eight services and three surfaces, each number downstream of the one
below it.

4.3 A Reusable Pattern

The shape worth carrying to any similar brief is the projection over read-only record systems: adapters
subscribe, the model links, services compute, surfaces propose, a person commits. A team reusing it
swaps the interoperability standard for whatever their site already runs, swaps the object set for their own
assets and records, and swaps the models within their own origin and licensing rules. What they keep is
the discipline that makes the shape hold: machines are never written to, no system of record is replaced,
the only write path is a person-approved record, and the first gate proves the joins on live production data
before any analytics is trusted.

Fourteen Objects Turn Depot Data Into One Argument

Power pack, vehicle hull, machine tool, test cell, work order, part lot and operator role
become fourteen typed objects whose links let one query walk from a failed test run back to
the part lot and the machine that cut it.

Chapter 4 showed the stack as layers with fixed counts. This chapter opens the middle layer, where
fourteen typed objects turn record systems that never shared a key into one argument a planner can
query.

5.1 Fourteen Objects and Their Links

Four objects carry asset identity: the power pack, the vehicle hull, the machine tool and the power pack
test cell, joined by the machine sensor as the instrumented asset and the edge gateway as the system
object that carries its traffic. Three carry intent as records: the production work order, the maintenance
work order and the schedule proposal. The rest are one each by kind: the part lot as material, the test run
as event, the run report as document, the operator role as actor, and the condition indicator as measure.
Figure 4 draws every object and its typed links. The links are what a document store cannot hold: an out-

condition indicators. One query walks from a failed test run to the machine that cut the failing part and the
vibration baseline it was running against, crossing four systems of record in a single traversal; in a
document store every hop is a separate search against a separate index, and the hops are exactly where
the trace dies today. Table 8 below anchors each object in its system of record and lists its typed links.

5.2 The Human Loop and the Hosting Posture

The loop lives in status vocabularies, not in prose. A maintenance work order moves through Proposed,
Approved, Scheduled, In work, Complete or Declined, and only a planner moves it; a schedule proposal
is accepted, modified or declined by the planner it names; a run report stays draft until the test cell
operator signs it, and only a signed report publishes over OPC UA. The operator role object carries the
qualification and sign-off authority that makes each of those signatures mean something. The hosting
posture is fixed by the requirement itself: everything runs on the depot's own government hardware inside
the facility's security rules, data and models stay in the government's own environment, identity is issued
on site through Keycloak, there is no external link and no third-party model service, and one-way transfer
hardware is the only path by which anything would ever leave. The only write path out of the platform is

the person-approved record: work raised in the maintenance system, and the signed run report. No
machine or site control is ever written to.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 6

Five Sources Enter Through One Adapter Family

Every source system arrives through the integration adapter family over the site's OPC UA
standard and MTConnect taps, with the event backbone preserving order and buffering
through outages so no machine is ever written to.

Chapter 5 described what the model holds. This chapter describes how data gets into it: five source
systems, all of them the operator's own, all arriving through one adapter family that never writes to a
machine.

6.1 Five Sources and Their Provenance

Figure 5 maps them. The production control system, the operator's own system of record for rebuild and
rework, contributes the work order and routing objects, read only. The inventory system owns the part lots
the reject trace must reach. The maintenance system owns the machine asset register and work order
history, and it also receives: the design's own loop ends as work raised there for a planner to approve,
though that write is a person-approved record rather than a machine interface. The test cell software
holds the test runs and the run reports. The OPC UA site standard is the fifth source and the
interoperability path in both directions: machine and test cell state is subscribed read-only over it, and the
signed run report publishes back over it. NIST defines interoperability as the ability of two system
components to communicate correctly and completely with each other, and notes how rarely the word is
met in practice (NIST n.d.). The design therefore rides the standard the site already runs rather than
inventing a parallel one.

          Figure 5. The 5 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

6.2 What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

One adapter family, built on the Open62541 OPC UA stack, carries every source, and its guarantees are
fixed. Every interface is a read-only subscription, in every phase, with no write to the site or any machine.
Identity is checked on site before any subscription opens. Each message carries provenance, so every
property in the object model traces back to the record system that owns it, and where two systems do not
share a key a supervised crosswalk is built and owned in the ontology with lineage rather than silently
matched. Legacy machines join the network the same way, through stack light and serial taps beside the
controller, additive and reversible, replacing nothing.

6.3 The Event Backbone

Apache Kafka 4.3 with KRaft runs the backbone inside the site. Ordering is per key: every event for one
machine or one test run is totally ordered, so a scripted cycle's parameter sequence never reorders in the
store. Delivery is at-least-once with idempotent writes into InfluxDB 3 Core and the object model, so a
replay cannot double-count a part lot. Buffering lives at the edge: each machine-group gateway holds
events through a network outage and catches up when the link returns, and its clock offset and last sync
are themselves visible objects. Time comes from a PTP grandmaster through linuxptp, because a store
that merges sensor streams on a sloppy clock cannot support a trace. Replication stays inside the site, on
the depot's own hardware. The posture is earned from the industry's own losses: a simple update to a
parts ordering system halted Toyota's production (Automotive Manufacturing Solutions 2023) at an
estimated 350 million US dollars (ABI Research 2023), and because this design is additive and read-only
against every machine, the worst it can do to production is stop reporting on it.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 7

Forecasting Lives at the Edge, Reasoning in the Server
Room

Condition scoring and vibration acquisition run on fanless edge boxes beside each machine
group, the 117-billion-parameter work surface model runs on the depot's own two-card
inference server, and only derived states cross the boundary between them.

Chapter 6 described how five source systems enter through adapters and an event backbone without any
of them surrendering control of its records. This chapter describes where the computing happens once
the data is inside, and why the split between the machine cabinet and the server room is a load-bearing
decision rather than a convenience.

7.1 Three Tiers, Each Sized for Its Own Duty

The design places inference at three tiers. At the edge, fanless DIN-rail industrial computers sit beside
each machine group and at the test cell, running the vibration acquisition channels, the controller state
subscriptions and the first-pass condition scoring; the forecasting model that carries that scoring,
Chronos-2, occupies about 0.48 GB at 32 bit as published and about 0.24 GB at 16 bit, which leaves the
bulk of a fanless unit's memory for waveform capture at tens of kilosamples per second. The vibration
acquisition load on this unit is unmeasured, so a dev board measurement of the actual channel count and
sample rate is the phase one gate before the edge class is fixed, and the PCIe accelerator module is the
named growth path if the measurement lands high. At the site tier, the same forecasting model runs in an
analytics role beside the embedding model and the time series store. At the top, the agentic work surface
model runs on the depot's own inference server: two cards of the 48 GB PCIe class, air-cooled in the
depot's server room on its existing power, drawing about 700 W of card power between them. The
memory arithmetic comes from the published checkpoint: the 117 billion parameters ship as about 65.2
GB, the MoE weights in MXFP4 and the rest at 16 bit; multiplied by 1.2 to reserve room for the KV cache
and activations, the cards must hold about 78.2 GB, against 96 GB of memory on two 48 GB cards and
roughly 88 GB usable after the serving runtime takes its share, about 10 GB of headroom. The KV cache
ceiling that remains is enough for the planner-facing sessions the work surface actually serves, and no
larger model is committed. Figure 6 sets the three tiers side by side with what runs on each.

        Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.

7.2 The Latency Budget

The budget is set by the fastest consumer of each signal, and the design's read-only posture removes the
tightest class from the budget entirely: because no machine or test cell interface ever writes to a control,
there is no control-loop latency to guarantee, only an observation and advisory one. Continuous
transducer and data bus reads must arrive in order and with a trustworthy timestamp, which is why the
design carries a PTP grandmaster of the OCP Time Card class and boundary or transparent clock
support on every hop between it and the edge boxes, since an unmeasured queueing delay would spend
the whole time error budget. Condition scoring wants to land near the machine so a rising indicator is
visible within the shift. The work surface and the scheduling proposals it drafts serve planners, so its
latency tolerance is human, measured in how long a planner waits for a drafted schedule, not in
milliseconds; the same holds for the run report, which is produced at the end of a scripted test cycle and
signed off by a person before anything is published.

7.3 What Crosses the Boundary, and What Each Failure Costs

The network boundary between the edge boxes and the site tier is crossed by derived states, not raw
waveforms: condition indicators with their zones, machine state, test run outcomes and signed run
reports, all carried on the event backbone toward the object model, and run reports publish onward over
the site's OPC UA interoperability standard. When the link fails, the edge boxes keep working and catch
up: each gateway object records its buffered events, clock offset and last sync, and resynchronizes on
recovery, so a dark uplink delays visibility rather than losing it. When power fails, Network UPS Tools
rides the units through the gap and the buffers absorb the rest. When the update path is exercised,
artifacts move through the Harbor registry under the air-gapped transfer discipline, with Lidi handling any
one-way transfer out of the enclave, so no update channel doubles as an inbound path. None of these
failures reaches a machine control, because none of these paths writes to one.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 8

The License Terms Decide What the Depot Owns

Three Apache-2.0 models from US publishers carry forecasting, retrieval and the agentic
work surface, and the plainness of the license is what lets the depot hold its own weights
inside the government boundary rather than rent them back.

Chapter 7 fixed where each model runs and proved the two-card server holds the work surface with
headroom. This chapter turns to the terms under which those weights are held at all, because on a
government site the license is not fine print: it decides whether the depot owns its intelligence or rents it
back. Figure 7 sets out the model stack in one view, and its shape follows from a single constraint stated
in the operator's own words: the models are US origin open weights, with no third-party model service.
Three models, all Apache-2.0, all from US publishers, satisfy that constraint outright. The work surface
model is gpt-oss-120b, a 117-billion-parameter mixture of experts published by OpenAI and filed under
the 300-billion-parameter threshold that would have forced a frontier cluster class. Its checkpoint is 60.8
GiB, with the MoE weights in MXFP4 at 4.25 bits and the remainder at 16 bit; its role is agentic work
surface and ontology maintenance, running on the site inference server described in Chapter 7, where it
carries Pragma's agents over the ontology, the run reports and the maintenance histories. It was chosen
because the requirement's US-origin rule sets aside the house GLM class, whose publisher's US Entity
List listing would bar it for this site regardless of fit. Apache-2.0 imposes no field-of-use restriction and no
per-seat trigger, so the depot holds the weights as property. The forecasting model is Chronos-2, a zero-
shot multivariate forecaster with covariate support under Apache-2.0 from a US publisher. It occupies
about 0.48 GB at 32 bit and about 0.24 GB at 16 bit, which is why it fits both the machine-group edge
boxes and the site analytics tier. Its role is machine condition forecasting and residual anomaly detection:
baselines and thresholds are computed per machine class from live data, and no weights are ever
trained, which is the system of context rule for this site. The retrieval model is nomic-embed-text-v2-moe,
a 475-million-parameter Apache-2.0 embedder from a US publisher, with Matryoshka truncation to 256
dimensions so the depot's work order, maintenance and test report corpus fits the site index. All 475
million parameters stay resident because every expert is exercised; the footprint is about 0.95 GB at
FP16 and about 0.5 GB at 8 bit. The other embedders considered that are large enough for this job are of
Chinese origin and barred by the same rule that set aside the GLM class.

PA R T I I I · C H A P T E R 9

A Week of Live Joins Comes Before Any Trust

Phase one is sixteen items across six workstreams ending in a gate that proves entity
resolution on a week of live records with a stated match rate, and phase two carries the
estate instrumentation rollout only after that gate holds.

Chapter 8 settled the models and the licenses that let the depot hold its own weights on its own
government hardware. This chapter sequences the build so that the joins are proven on live records
before any alarm, trace or proposal is trusted, and it names the gates that can stop the work cheaply.

9.1 Two Phases, Sixteen Items and One Gate

Phase one carries 16 items across six workstreams: Connected depot, Depot object model, Machine
condition, Phasing, Power pack test cell, and Reject traceability and scheduling. The items include the
depot operating object model core, entity resolution across the unshared keys, and the read-only machine
data backbone over OPC UA, alongside the test cell instrumentation, the condition baselining per
machine class, the reject trace through part lots, and the schedule proposals a planner decides. The
phase ends at a single exit gate: entity resolution proven across one week of live production records, with

the power pack serial, the machine asset tag, the part lot and the test run identifier, four keys no system
of record shares, joined at a stated match rate. Phase two carries one item, the estate instrumentation
rollout, and it is admitted only once that gate holds. Requirement coverage stands at two requirements
covered, none partial and none open, and Figure 8 sets the phases, their item counts, their workstreams
and the gate against that coverage.

             Figure 8. The two phases and their gates, and coverage of the 2 requirements across them.

9.2 What the Rollout Measures

Every gate in this build is a measurement, not an assertion. The match rate across the four identifiers is
measured on the week of live records before any crosswalk is accepted, and where a key does not exist,
the supervised crosswalk built in its place carries lineage and an owner. Baseline stability is measured
per machine class and per machine, so a fan and a spindle are never held to one threshold. Alarm
precision is measured by checking elevated and alarm zones against what maintenance actually finds
when work is raised. The disagreement rate between operator-entered downtime and reject reason codes
and machine state taken from the controller taps is measured continuously, because that rate is itself a
signal about data quality rather than a fact to be filed. Clock offset and buffered event count are read from
each edge gateway, and the open-format run report is checked for fidelity as published over the site's
OPC UA standard.

9.4 Lessons

Prove the joins before the analytics. The whole design rests on one projection over four systems that
never shared a key, so the week of live records and its match rate come first, and no condition indicator,
reject trace or schedule proposal is trusted ahead of them; the documented cost of an integration fault in
this sector is measured in hundreds of millions of dollars (ABI Research 2023), and a gate that costs a
week of records is cheap insurance against that cost.

Instrument only the machines whose failures announce themselves. Condition monitoring on a
machine with no wear-out zone buys nothing and calendar removal of such items can add infant-mortality
failures, so classification by failure pattern and consequence precedes every sensor purchase, and the
register records where the answer is to leave the calendar alone.

Keep the enclave small enough to assess. A controlled unclassified information boundary scoped late
stops a program rather than slowing it, so the enclave is scoped in phase one with named owners, and
everything that does not need to touch the drawings, programs and test data stays outside it.

Treat reason codes as a signal, not a fact. Operator-entered codes decay, so the design never reasons
from them alone; it reasons from machine state and treats the disagreement between the two as a
monitored quantity a planner can see.

9.5 What Is Still Open

Three questions remain open, and each has a named settling path. The match-rate threshold that
constitutes a pass at the gate is set with the depot's planners once the week of live records is in view, and
settling it fixes how much crosswalk effort phase two inherits. The controlled unclassified information
determination for the drawings, programs and test data rests with the site authorizing official, and settling
it fixes the enclave boundary and therefore the assessment scope. The dev board measurement of
vibration acquisition load fixes the edge hardware class or moves it to the PCIe accelerator module, and
settling it fixes the per-machine-group bill of materials for the estate instrumentation rollout.

PA R T I I I · C H A P T E R 1 0

The Depot Owns the Model and Its Memory

The object model, the per-class baselines, the decision record and the hardware all belong to
the depot, which means the intelligence compounds inside the government boundary instead
of leaving it with every improvement.

Chapter 9 showed how the build earns trust one gate at a time. This chapter settles who holds what the
build produces, because a system that compounds learning inside a government boundary is worth
nothing if every improvement walks out of it.

10.1 What the Depot Owns

The object model belongs to the depot. It is a projection over the production control, inventory,
maintenance and test cell systems, but the projection, the crosswalks and their lineage are assets the
depot keeps, expressed in its own vocabulary and re-pointable if a system of record is ever replaced. The
weights belong to the depot as well: every model in the design is an Apache-2.0 open-weight model of US
origin, held on the depot's own government hardware, and because nothing in this design is trained or
fine-tuned into weights, the improving assets are the per-machine-class baselines, the alarm thresholds
and the failure mode register, all of which are data the depot produced and owns outright. The decision
record belongs to the depot: every sign-off on a run report, every planner acceptance, modification or
decline of a schedule proposal, and every maintenance work order approved or declined is a kept record
the next decision reads, so the memory of how the depot actually judges its own machines stays with the
depot. The boundary belongs to the depot: the edge boxes, the site inference server and the work surface
run on government hardware inside the facility's security rules, updates arrive through a one-way transfer
path, and no data or model leaves the boundary to any third-party service.

10.2 The Offer Behind the Design

CodeNinja builds this shape under five names, and this design maps to each of them: Adaptive
Operations is the sensing and forecasting of physical behavior, the transducer and data bus reads in the
test cell and the vibration, spindle load and temperature trending on the machine tools; Decision Systems
is the ranking, attribution and recommendation a named person decides, the reject trace through part lots,
the schedule proposals a planner accepts or declines, and the maintenance work a planner approves;
Hyper Ontology is the object model itself, the projection over the four systems of record; Hyper Pragma is
the work surface on which the depot's own planners and engineers build and run their agents; and
Sovereign Infrastructure is the posture the whole design takes, own government hardware, Apache-2.0
open-weight models of US origin, and operation inside the facility's security boundary with no third-party
model service. Praxis is the platform on which the design was produced, and Chapter 11 traces how.

PA R T I V · C O N C L U S I O N

The Same Shape Joins Any Set of Record Systems
In one view, the design is a read-only projection: five systems of record keep their authority, one object
model of fourteen types joins them across keys they never shared, edge boxes watch machines without
touching their controls, models forecast and reason inside the government boundary, and every release,
work order and schedule change lands on a named person's decision.

Running the same shape elsewhere takes three things rather than a new architecture: an entity resolution
gate proved on a week of live records before any analytics is trusted, per-class baselines and a failure
mode register instead of trained weights, and licenses plain enough that the operator can hold its own
weights on its own hardware, wherever the systems of record are the only things that differ.

PA R T I V · C H A P T E R 11

How Praxis Contextualized and Reasoned This Design

Every design in this series is produced on Praxis, and this chapter traces each choice in the
paper back to the recorded reading that justified it, through the eight lenses and the patterns
they returned.

Chapter 10 settled ownership, and it closed by naming the platform that produced the design. This
chapter opens the record of that work, so a reader can trace any choice in this paper back to the recorded
reading that justified it (Figure 9). Every design in the Vertical-Driven Architectures series is produced on
Praxis, and this chapter is the trace for this one. Nothing in it is reconstructed after the fact: the ask, the
reading and the patterns below are the recorded basis of the choices the paper has presented.

11.1 Contextualizing the Ask

The ask reached Praxis in the operator's own words: one operating object model across a United States
discrete manufacturing and automotive operator, with power pack, vehicle hull, machine tool, test cell,
work order, part lot and operator role each linked to its system of record; legacy machine tools and test
equipment brought onto the network read only; the power pack test cell as the first live case with scripted
cycles, continuous transducer and data bus reads, automatic open-format run reports published over the
site's industrial interoperability standard, and a person's sign-off on every release; predictive maintenance
on machine tools from live process data; reject causes traced through the model; scheduling proposals a
planner decides; and, binding everything, a United States government site, US-origin open weights and
named federal information security approvals. Praxis assigned the design to the Physical AI family in the
Discrete Manufacturing and Automotive industry. In the room were the operator's stated requirement, read
in full; the shelf of stack cards carrying the tooling choices with their versions; the model register with
verified parameter counts, footprints, precisions and licenses; the hardware class register with its sizing
rules; and the recorded failure-mode notes that became Table 5. The requirement was read in full; of 961
shelf records listed, 132 were read in full; all are available on request.

11.3 Patterns Adopted and Set Aside

The patterns adopted are the ones the paper has argued: the projection ontology over four systems of
record instead of point-to-point interfaces, because the failure is one of vocabulary that more interfaces
reproduce; the read-only subscription backbone over OPC UA with no write to any machine or site
control; per-machine-class baselines and thresholds instead of any trained weights; and edge buffering
with catch-up after an outage, beside the machines it watches. The patterns set aside are equally
recorded: the labeling and retraining pipeline is not built, because nothing is trained into weights and
improvement runs through memory loops; camera tracking and people or vehicle positioning are not built,
because crews, hulls and power packs are tracked through work orders, test runs and part lots rather
than worn tags; no frontier 300B to 1T parameter cluster is designed, because the committed work
surface model sits at 117B parameters under the US-origin constraint; a vendor cloud predictive
maintenance service is set aside for the same rule that bars third-party model service; and the house
default open-weight class of Chinese origin is set aside for the operator's own US-origin requirement.

11.4 Where the Reasoning Lands

The reasoning lands on four equipment classes that carry the machine condition duty: the spindle IEPE
accelerometer class mounted per ISO 5348, the spindle current clamp classes for motor current signature
analysis, the legacy machine retrofit tap classes for stack light and serial DPRNT taps, and the plant floor
edge compute class, fanless and DIN-rail mounted, whose vibration acquisition load is the phase one
measurement before the class is fixed. Around them sit the 48 GB PCIe inference class holding the work
surface model at its native 4-bit build, the hardened managed switch class with PTP clock support on
every hop, and the time card grandmaster class that anchors the clocks the joins depend on. Every
choice in this chapter, and therefore every choice in this paper, traces to recorded reading: the
requirement in the operator's words, the stack shelf, the model register, the hardware register and the
lens notes. Nothing shown was inferred, and nothing in the design rests on a source this paper has not
cited.

title: Port Drone Watch: From Oil Sheen to Dispatched Work on the Port's Own Hardware in Germany
text:
VERTICAL-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURES · MARITIME & PORTS · DESIGNED WITH PRAXIS · OCTOBER 2026

Port Drone Watch: From Oil Sheen to
Dispatched Work on the Port's Own
Hardware in Germany
For a maritime and ports authority in Germany, a physical AI system that turns the docked
drone network at its two port sites into detections, dispatched work items and a living map,
running entirely on the authority's own hardware.

Muhammad Umar, Cofounder, CodeNinja

For the authority's operations and security directors, the harbour, inspection and marine services leads, and the
platform, data and computer vision engineers who would build and run it.

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-
world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for
designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

ABSTRACT

A Detection Should Reach a Responder, Not a Video
Archive
For a maritime and ports authority in Germany, the question a physical AI system must answer is
deceptively simple: what is happening right now on the water, the quays and the restricted zones of its
two port sites, and which named person should respond. Drones already fly from docks at both sites and
land hours of video and still imagery every day, but nobody can watch all of it, so oil sheen drifts, persons
cross restricted zones, fenders and bollards fail and works packages slip while the footage sits
unreviewed. The answer must also satisfy three regimes at once: the European specific category drone
rules that govern every flight, the Seveso directives that fence the hazardous installations the drones
overfly, and the GDPR rules that protect every person the cameras catch in frame.

The design turns those flights into detections and dispatched work entirely on the authority's own
hardware: five source systems enter through one adapter family, fifteen objects form one typed object

model, five services and eight surfaces carry the work, and five models are placed across three tiers. Per-
frame closed-set detection runs on the dock's edge compute so that detection survives an uplink loss;
zero-shot open-vocabulary passes and evidence-crop triage run on the port's site servers; and the
frontier-class work surface model, 753 billion parameters at FP8 held by one node of eight GPUs of the
141 GB class, runs in the port's own data centre. Every detection becomes a work item with a named
responder role, people decide every response, and the loop learns from what responders found through
memory rather than weight training, so the imagery, the weights and the detection history survive a
change of drone operator.

The paper covers the industry problem and the join failure in Part I; the constraints, the stack, the object
model, ingestion, inference placement, and the models and their licences in Part II; the rollout with its
phases and gates, and ownership, in Part III; and it closes with how Praxis contextualised and reasoned
the design. Readers weighing industrial ontology examples will find every object and typed link in chapter
5.

 Figure 1. Port Drone Watch on one page: the sources the operation already runs, one object model, what it computes,
                                            and the person who decides.

Contents

         Conclusion · The Port Owns the Eyes It Already Flies                        Executive

 11      Praxis Recorded Every Choice This Design Stands On                          Team Lead     FDE

         Sources                                                                     Reference

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

Hours of Drone Imagery Answer No One's Question

The authority already flies drones that produce hours of imagery a day across two port sites,
yet the question that matters, what is happening right now and who should respond, goes
unanswered because the footage outruns every pair of human eyes.

The abstract promised a port authority turning its existing drone flights into detections, dispatched work
and a living map, entirely on its own hardware. This chapter states the question that promise answers, the
documented cost of leaving it unanswered, and the scenario the design serves.

1.1 The Question and the Ground It Stands On

The authority needs one question answered continuously across its two port sites: what is happening
right now, where exactly is it happening, and which named person should respond. Answering it requires
data the operation already holds in fragments: hours of drone imagery and still images produced every
day by scheduled and on-demand missions, the berth plan and asset register held in its geographic
information system, the vessel traffic picture from the automatic identification system (AIS) and the vessel
traffic service (VTS), its works records, and the weather observations that decide whether a flight can
launch at all. Three regulatory regimes frame every part of the answer. Flights run under the European
specific category drone rules, under which operations beyond the open category require operational
authorisation tied to assessed risk, so every mission carries a flight authorisation reference and a
geofence. Some zones sit inside Seveso perimeters, the European major-hazard regime around sites
holding dangerous substances, which imposes approval requirements and responder-within-minutes
rules the design must route detections around. And because the cameras photograph people, the whole
imagery pipeline stands on the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the European data
protection framework: persons in restricted zones are detections to act on and personal data to process
lawfully, with retention, signage and a processing map as first-order requirements, not afterthoughts.

1.2 The Documented Cost of Not Knowing

The cost of an unanswered waterline is documented, and it is measured in lives and fines. A peer-
reviewed Bayesian network analysis of 505 maritime occupational accident cases traces how such
accidents arise (Yu et al. 2025), and the US safety institute NIOSH holds that marine terminal and port
workers carry higher fatality, injury and illness rates than other workers (CDC 2024). Pollution carries its
own ledger: a shipping company was fined 2 million dollars for a maritime pollution offence in a single
prosecution (US Department of Justice 2025), and a US safety investigation established the probable
cause of a bulker's crash into a barge (TradeWinds 2021). Against that background, oil sheen that drifts
for a day before anyone reviews footage, a person in a restricted zone noticed only in yesterday's
recording, and quay damage found at annual inspection rather than at the next flight are not inefficiencies;
they are latent incidents. The International Labour Organization now maintains an experimental global
register of fatalities at sea covering occupational accidents, persons overboard and health-related deaths
(ILO 2025), which is the scale of loss the register exists to reduce.

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

The operation is a maritime and ports authority in Germany running two port sites, two places with distinct
traffic, quays and hazard perimeters. Its drones are a docked network: aircraft that live in automated
stations and launch on a schedule or on demand, flown by a retained drone operator under the European
specific category. The fleet carries several payload classes, among them a patrol nadir camera, a berth
survey camera and an incident response camera, with a thermal payload held as a named annual trial
rather than day-one scope. Missions produce hours of imagery and still images every day, in salt air, wind
and visibility conditions that ground flights and open multi-day coverage gaps. The people in the loop are
few and named by role: flight approvers who grant authorisations, responder roles that own detection

classes by domain, security, inspection, spill and vapour response, with shift cover and escalation paths,
and the drone operator's own crew. The design draws on five source systems, four of them the port's own
or its operator's, and produces eight detection classes: oil sheen, floating debris, moored vessels, berth
occupancy, open gates, persons in restricted zones, fender or bollard damage, and smoke or vapour. The
chapters that follow turn those flights into answers.

Sovereignty and Seveso Shape Every Downstream
Choice

Port-owned hardware, the European specific category drone rules, Seveso perimeters and
GDPR together force the design's scoping decisions, each of which buys something and
costs something this chapter prices in the open.

Chapter 2 showed that the failure is a join failure, not a data failure. This chapter states the goals that
shape how the design makes that join, and prices the scoping decisions each goal forces.

3.1 Everything Runs on the Authority's Own Hardware and Survives a Change of Drone
Operator

The first constraint is ownership: all compute sits inside the port authority's own environment on its own
hardware, and mission data lands in the port's own systems. This is hard in this industry because the
drone operator naturally holds missions and imagery in its own estate, and a six-year service will outlive
operator contracts. Sovereign here means self-hosted, not small: the design runs per-frame detection at
the dock, reasoning on port servers, and the imagery, the models and the detection history belong to the

port, so a change of drone operator is a data-handover event the exit obligations are written around, not a
rebuild.

3.2 Every Detection Becomes a Work Item with a Named Responder

The second constraint is the loop: people decide every response, and the platform proposes and records.
It is hard because responders already live in their own work systems, so the design must own the work
item, with its evidence frames, confidence, location and responder finding, and push records outward
rather than demand that responders move. The acknowledgement is itself a decision object with reason
codes, because the responder's finding is the most valuable data the loop collects.

3.3 Flights Obey the Specific Category and Seveso Perimeters

The third constraint is flight law: every mission runs under the European specific category with an
authorisation, a geofence and zones whose approval requirements and responder-within-minutes rules
the dispatch logic must honour, and some of those perimeters are Seveso sites. This is hard because the
rules bind the design's own plumbing: a detection inside a Seveso zone cannot wait in a generic queue,
and a weather grounding must publish what the gap blinded, not leave silence that reads as an absence
of findings.

3.4 Persons in Frame Are Governed by GDPR

The fourth constraint is data protection: there is no domestic licence for camera use, and persons in
frame are personal data from the moment of capture. This is hard because the simplest architecture,
streaming everything and keeping everything, is unlawful. The processing map, retention covenant and
signage are first-phase deliverables, retention defaults to days with automatic, demonstrable deletion,
and the design improves through memory rather than weight training, so no responder finding ever
becomes a training corpus.

4.1 The Pattern and Why It Fits

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 5

Fifteen Objects Turn Drone Frames Into One Argument

Fifteen objects and their typed links let a query walk from a frame to a detection to a berth to
a responder role, a journey across mission, asset, actor and record that no document store
can make.

The stack placed one object model at its centre and named it as the place where the port's argument is
held. This chapter opens that model: fifteen objects, their typed links, the human loop that lives inside
them and the posture that keeps them the port's own.

5.1 Every Object and the Links Between Them

The fifteen objects divide into six kinds. Two are events: Mission and Construction Work. Four are
records: Detection, Work Item, Flight Authorisation and Coverage Statement. Three are sites: Berth, Dock
Station and Restricted Zone. Three are assets: Vessel, Quay Asset and Drone. Two are actors:
Responder Role and Drone Operator. One is a measure: Weather Observation. Figure 4 shows every
object and every typed link between them, with the Mission object, the one the most links reach, in focus.

The links are what make the model an argument rather than a filing system. A Mission is launched from a
Dock Station and crosses Restricted Zones under a Flight Authorisation. A Detection is produced by a
mission and carries its frames and timestamps. A Work Item is dispatched to a responder role. A Vessel
occupies a Berth, and the Berth sits on a Quay Asset, and Construction Work progresses on that same

quay. A Coverage Statement declares which detection classes a weather grounding blinded, so an
absence of findings is never mistaken for an absence of events. This matters because port work is
dangerous work: workers in marine terminals and port operations have higher fatality, injury and illness
rates than other workers (CDC 2024), and a damage finding that cannot reach a named responder is a
finding the port does not have.

The payoff is the query. When an operator asks what changed on a quay since last week, the walk goes
from the Quay Asset to its Berths, to the Vessels occupying them, to the Construction Work recorded
against it, to the Detections confirmed on it, to the responder findings behind each, all in one traversal
across mission, asset, actor and record. A document store cannot make this journey: it can find
documents that mention the quay, but each hop to the vessel, the work package or the responder is
another lookup with no guaranteed linkage, and the joins must be written in advance for every question
rather than expressed once as typed links.

           Figure 4. The fifteen objects of the model and the typed links that let a query reach across them.

5.2 The Human Loop and the Hosting Posture

The human loop lives in the status vocabularies. A Detection is Proposed until a responder confirms it,
rejects it or merges it with an earlier finding. A Work Item is Dispatched, then Acknowledged with reason
codes, then Resolved or Closed no action. Acknowledgement is itself a decision object, so acknowledge
rate, ignore rate and action rate are measurable from the first week, and the disagreement path is built
before the agreement path. The system proposes and records; people decide every response, and its
automatic acts are limited to confirmation re-flights and notification escalation.

The hosting posture follows the constraints. Every object, every frame and every model runs on the port
authority's own hardware inside its own boundary. Identity is issued through Keycloak to named people in
named roles. The single external link is the controlled ingest of the drone operator's mission data. The
one write path into the object model runs through the adapter tier and the surfaces used by authenticated
responders. The loop learns from what responders found through agentic memory, never by training
weights, so the detection history and the improvement both belong to the port and survive a change of
drone operator.

Every Source Enters Through an Adapter, Never Directly

Five named source systems, from the drone operator's mission and fleet system to the
vessel traffic feed, reach the object model only through the integration adapter family, which
holds the guarantees the port's own systems stay authoritative.

Chapter 5 described what the object model holds and who writes to it. This chapter describes how data
gets there: five named source systems, one adapter family, and an event backbone that keeps every
frame, event and record ordered, timestamped and replayable.

6.1 Five Sources and Their Provenance

Five source systems feed the model, and Figure 5 maps each to its provenance class and its adapter
path. The port GIS berth plan and asset register is an authority-provenance source, read only: the living
map builds on it, and this project standardises it and publishes the governed layer back, so the port's own
spatial data becomes the deliverable rather than being replaced by a bought one. The drone operator's
mission and fleet system is an authority-provenance source, read only: the docks and drones are
retained, and mission data landing in the port's own systems is a stated requirement, so flights, telemetry
and imagery flow in through a controlled ingest. The responders' existing work systems are authority-

provenance, read for status: this system owns the work item and pushes records out to them, so
responders keep working in their own tools. The vessel traffic feed, AIS and VTS, is domain-typical
provenance, read only: moored vessel and berth occupancy detections are checked against the
authority's own vessel picture rather than imagery alone. The fifth source, the port's works register and
weather feed, has its provenance confirmed at the interface survey before it is committed.

       Figure 5. The 5 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

6.2 What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

One family, the integration adapter, stands between every source and the object model, and it carries five
guarantees. First, authority: the port's systems remain the masters of their facts, and the ontology is a
projection, so a berth plan revision in GIS supersedes the projected berth, never the reverse. Second,
provenance: every event is stamped with its source system and provenance class, so any detection can
be traced to the mission, frame and model version that produced it. Third, isolation: schema drift in a
source is absorbed in the adapter, not in the object model. Fourth, replay: because adapters write to the
log, any object can be rebuilt from recorded events. Fifth, fallback: if the drone operator's interfaces prove
closed or undocumented, an interface survey in the first workstream either opens them or falls back to
dock-side capture of the video stream with telemetry by file drop, and the guarantee that mission data
reaches the port's own systems holds either way.

6.3 The Event Backbone

Apache Kafka 4.3, running in KRaft mode without a separate coordination service, is the backbone every
adapter writes to. Ordering is per partition key: events for one mission and one asset are strictly ordered,
which is what lets a detection cite the frame that produced it and a work item cite the detection. Delivery is
at-least-once, and writes into the object model are idempotent, keyed on mission and frame timestamps,
so a replayed event creates no duplicate detection. Buffering lives at the dock: the edge box under K3s
retains events and MediaMTX recordings locally through an uplink loss, so detection continues and the
backlog resynchronises when the link returns, which is the doctrine that detection survives an uplink loss.
Replication runs between brokers in the port's own data centre, inside the boundary. Model and artifact

updates arrive through Harbor as an air-gapped registry, so nothing enters by ad hoc transfer. All of it
rides one clock: linuxptp with chrony, disciplined by an OCP Time Card grandmaster, keeps drone frames,
telemetry and vessel traffic records aligned, and Prometheus, Grafana and Loki watch the backbone's lag
and health so a silent gap becomes an alarm, not a coverage hole discovered later.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 7

Detection Belongs at the Dock, Reasoning on Port
Servers

Per-frame closed-set detection runs on the dock's edge box because pixels cannot cross the
uplink and detection must survive its loss, while zero-shot passes, evidence triage and the
frontier work surface run on the port's own servers under an explicit latency budget.

Chapter 6 described how every source enters through the integration adapter, so that missions, imagery
references, vessel positions and responder records all arrive as governed events in one backbone. This
chapter describes where the thinking happens: which model runs on which tier of the authority's own
hardware, how fast each answer must arrive, and what survives when the dock's uplink, its power or its
update path fails.

7.1 Three Tiers and the Arithmetic That Places Them

The design runs inference on three tiers, and Figure 6 sets them side by side. The first tier is the dock's
edge box, an edge AI compute module of the GPU class sized by the dock site survey against salt air,
wind and temperature. It runs the per-frame closed-set detector, RF-DETR, over the retained drone fleet's
camera streams for moored vessels, buoys, persons, vehicles and gates, together with the Roboflow
trackers for motion and association, all orchestrated as containers under K3s with MediaMTX handling
ingest and recording. Per-frame detection belongs here for one reason: hours of video and still imagery
every day cannot cross the dock uplink, so the pixels are examined where they land and only events and
evidence crops travel onward.

The second tier is the site server at each port site, running one to four cards of the 48 GB PCIe inference
server class, air-cooled. It runs OWLv2 for zero-shot, open-vocabulary passes over selected frames,
covering oil sheen, floating debris, smoke or vapour and damage cues, and Ministral 3 8B under vLLM for
evidence-crop triage and work item drafting. Ministral 3 8B at FP8 occupies about 12 GB, which fits the
48 GB card with room for concurrent requests; it is treated strictly as a describer and reader of evidence,
never a localiser, because position comes from drone GNSS telemetry resolved against the standardised
berth plan.

The third tier is the central node the authority owns: one node of eight GPUs of the 141 GB HBM class,
1,128 GB in total, running GLM 5.3 as the agentic work surface over the ontology and memory. The sizing

line is explicit: 753 billion parameters at FP8, one byte per parameter, is 753 GB of weights; the 1.2
planning factor for KV cache and activations raises the requirement to 904 GB; the node's 1,128 GB
holds it, leaving roughly 375 GB beside the weights for KV cache and activations.

        Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.

7.2 The Latency Budget

The budget is stated as three classes of answer rather than one number. Per-frame detection must keep
pace with the camera stream itself, because a detector that falls behind the frames it is given produces a
delayed picture of a moving port. Detection-to-dispatch for persons in restricted zones and Seveso
perimeter events carries the responder-within-minutes rule, and the design routes those work items by the
zone's own rule; the stakes behind that budget are documented, since workers in marine terminals and
port operations carry higher fatality, injury and illness rates than other workers (CDC 2024). Queries on
the work surface, such as what changed on a quay since last week, are answered at conversational
speed from the ontology and memory on the central node.

7.3 What Crosses the Boundary, and What Fails Gracefully

What crosses the network boundary is deliberately small: detection events, evidence crops, telemetry and
health signals cross it; pixels do not. When the uplink fails, the dock keeps detecting, and the Kafka
backbone buffers events on the dock side for delivery and resynchronisation when the link returns. When
power fails, Network UPS Tools with the IP-rated dock enclosure and PoE budgeting carries the edge box
through the interruption and reports its state. When the update path fails, the air-gapped Harbor artifact
and model registry on the authority's own infrastructure holds the last good versions, and the site falls
back to them rather than to silence. Weather grounding is treated the same way honestly: each grounding
day publishes a coverage statement naming the detection classes that went blind, so responders never
mistake a coverage gap for an absence of findings.

Pilot Flights Come Before Any Detection Is Trusted

Four phases carrying twenty items move the service from two pilot missions on the port's
own imagery to a six-year operation, and no detection class rolls out below its measured
floor.

Chapter 8 fixed the model register and the licences that let the authority hold its own weights. This
chapter lays out the path from two pilot missions on the port's own imagery to a six-year operation: four
phases carrying twenty items, a gate on each phase that can stop the work cheaply, and the
measurements that decide whether any detection class earns the responders' trust.

9.1 Four Phases, Twenty Items, Four Gates

Phase 1 carries ten items across four workstreams: detection-to-dispatch, the flight-to-detection pipeline,
the living map and port standards, and the responder loop and learning. Its items include standing up

agentic memory over responder outcomes, standardising the berth plan and asset register for the quays
the pilot missions cover, and mapping responder roles with their dispatch rules. Its exit gate is the dock-
side edge inference hardware in place. Phase 2 carries four items across three workstreams and rolls out
the first port site's mission set; its items include geofencing the Seveso perimeters with gate approvals
and routing Seveso detections to a responder within minutes. Phase 3 carries four items across four
workstreams: extending detections to the second port site, pushing work records into the responders'
existing systems, and learning from what responders found. Its exit gate is port ownership secured
through a supplier change. Phase 4 carries two items across the responder loop and the sovereign
platform workstreams: running annual trial projects, beginning with the thermal night payload, without
rebuilding the platform, and operating the six-year service on the port authority's own hardware. Figure 8
sets the four phases side by side with their item counts, workstreams and gates. Requirement coverage is
complete: of the four requirements in the authority's ask, four are covered in full, none partial and none a
gap.

9.2 What the Rollout Measures

Pilot acceptance is measured on the port's own two missions, because pretrained and zero-shot
detectors are unproven on this port's imagery until its own drones fly it. No detection class rolls out below
its measured floor, and the floor must hold under drift with an operator-owned tuning path. On the
responder side, acknowledgement is a decision object with reason codes, so the acknowledge rate, the
ignore rate and the action rate are reported from the first dispatched work item onward; the disagreement
path is built before the agreement path. Weather grounding days are measured honestly through the pilot,
and every gap publishes a coverage statement naming its blind classes, so a grounded fleet reads as a
coverage gap rather than an absence of findings. Berth occupancy detections are checked against the
authority's own vessel picture rather than imagery alone.

9.4 Lessons

Publish the gaps you cannot fly through. A detection system that goes quiet in bad weather teaches
responders to read silence as safety, so the coverage statement is a first-class object with its own status
vocabulary, published by default and superseded only by a newer statement for the same area and
period.

Measure acceptance on the authority's own imagery. Vendor benchmarks on other ports' footage
settle nothing here, which is why the pilot's two missions on this port's own quays are the acceptance
basis and why every rollout is tied to a measured floor rather than a claimed one.

Make acknowledgement a decision, not a reflex. Responders in port operations already carry higher
fatality and injury rates than most other workers (CDC 2024), so a work item that is rubber-stamped

wastes their attention and corrupts the loop the service learns from; reason codes on every
acknowledgement keep the learning honest.

9.5 What Is Still Open

Three questions remain open. The weather source is to confirm, either the port's own weather station or
the national meteo service, and settling it fixes the go or no-go basis recorded on every weather
observation. The works register and the vessel traffic system are both to confirm as sources, and settling
them decides whether construction work and vessel objects are anchored in live feeds or in opening
balances. The edge silicon and its serving runtimes are fixed only at the dock site survey, and settling that
question fixes the per-frame detection budget at the dock. None of the three blocks the pilot; each blocks
a later phase, which is why each sits behind a gate.

PA R T I I I · C H A P T E R 1 0

The Detection History Survives a Change of Operator

The authority owns the object model, the open weights, the imagery and the full decision
record, and the drone operator object carries the exit handover obligations that make a
supplier change a non-event for the service.

Chapter 9 showed how the service earns trust phase by phase and what each gate measures. This
chapter settles the question the gates protect: who owns what the service produces, and why a change of
drone operator is a contract event rather than a rebuild.

10.1 Who Owns What the Design Builds

The object model is the authority's. Its fifteen objects, the typed links between them and the standardised
berth plan they sit on are built from the port's own GIS data inside this project, and the governed layer is
published back to the port's systems as its own spatial standard, so the living map is a port asset and not
a vendor fixture. The weights are the authority's. Every model in the register arrives under a licence that
permits the port to hold and run it: the vision detectors and the site-tier language model under Apache
2.0, the frontier work-surface model under its bespoke licence with commercial and internal use granted.
Nothing is trained into weights under the pinned architecture, so there are no fine-tunes to lose or re-
license; every threshold, routing rule and confidence band lives in memory as data the port owns and can
export. The decision record is the authority's. Every detection with its frames and confidence, every work
item with its named responder and finding, every flight authorisation and every coverage statement is a
recorded object, and the six-year history they accumulate is the evidence base the next decision reads.
The boundary is the authority's. All processing runs on the port authority's own hardware inside its own
environment; imagery crosses no external service, retention defaults to days with automatic deletion, and
the processing map is a phase-one item rather than a later disclosure. The drone operator object carries

the exit obligations that make this hold: the operator's name, the authorisations held under the European
specific category, the contract end date and the exit handover obligations, with a status vocabulary that
moves from in contract through notice period to changed. When it changes, the missions, drones and
stations change with it; the detections, the responders' findings and the map they are anchored to do not.

10.2 The Offer Behind the Design

CodeNinja builds the shape this paper describes: Adaptive Operations turns the retained drone fleet's
imagery into detections of physical behaviour, from oil sheen and smoke to berth occupancy and quay
wall damage; Decision Systems ranks every detection into a work item that a named responder decides
on, with the decision recorded; Hyper Ontology holds the fifteen-object model that anchors every
detection to a real quay, berth or asset; Hyper Pragma is the work surface where the authority's own
people build agents over that model and its memory; and Sovereign Infrastructure is the reason the whole
service runs on the authority's own hardware under open-weight licences inside its own boundary. The
design itself was produced on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for designing physical AI systems, and every
choice in it traces to the recorded reading the next chapter shows.

PA R T I V · C O N C L U S I O N

The Port Owns the Eyes It Already Flies
Taken in one view, the design is a projection over the port's own systems: drones and docks the authority
already runs feed frames to an edge box at the quay, detections rise into a fifteen-object model that links
every finding to its berth, its asset, its mission, its responder and its history, and five services push work
items into the systems responders already use while the port's own servers hold every weight and every
record. Nothing sits in front of the systems of record, and no automatic act goes beyond a confirmation
re-flight or a notification escalation.

The same shape travels: any operator with retained drone flights, a partial spatial register and existing
responder systems can stand it up, provided it standardises its own spatial data instead of buying a
replacement, commits to edge-first detection where the dock uplink is thin, keeps learning in memory
rather than in weights, and writes the supplier exit obligations into the service contract from the first day.

11.3 Patterns Adopted and Set Aside

Four patterns were adopted. Edge-first per-frame detection at the dock, with events and evidence crops
crossing the boundary rather than pixels, because hours of daily video cannot cross the dock uplink and
detection must survive its loss. Memory over weights, because the pinned architecture trains nothing and
improvement must survive a supplier change without a training run. The ontology as a projection beside
the systems of record, so the port's GIS and the responders' systems stay authoritative. Standardising the
port's own berth plan rather than buying a berth-management product, because the requirement asks for
occupancy against the port's own plan. Set aside with reasons: streaming all video to central servers,
rejected on uplink arithmetic; fine-tuning into weights, rejected by the architecture; fixed and thermal
cameras as day-one scope, thermal being a named annual trial and cameras being payloads on the
retained fleet; tag and anchor positioning for people, rejected because drone telemetry against the
standardised berth plan geo-locates every detection; and a one-way data diode, rejected because no
operational technology control zone is crossed.

11.4 Where the Reasoning Lands

The equipment classes the reasoning lands on are the 141 GB HBM GPU class, one node of eight cards
holding the frontier work-surface model at FP8 with the planning factor and KV cache beside the weights;
the 48 GB PCIe inference server class at the site tier, one to four air-cooled cards running the zero-shot
passes and the site language model; the open grandmaster time card with linuxptp and chrony, holding
one clock across sensors and systems; and the rugged enclosure, mounting and power class with
network UPS tools at the dock. Everything shown in this paper, from the doctrines to the model register to
these classes, was recorded reading on Praxis, and nothing in it is inferred.
